He is said to have reached the state of Nibbāna, which is well-described as "Deathless" (amata) because there is no death or because of its sublime meaning; as "Peace" (santi) because of the stilling of all formations; as "Nibbāna" because of the absence of the binding called craving; and as "Immovable" (accuta) because there is no falling away (death). Alternatively, it should be understood that the monk, being wise through the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and standing in the Fruit immediately following the Path, is called one who is faded away from desire and lust, and has reached the state of Nibbāna of the aforementioned nature. By the term "faded away from desire and lust," He shows that "this desire and lust has been abandoned by this monk, and this Fruit of Arahantship has been attained by him."

207-208. Having thus taught the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) together with its completion by way of the conscious and the unconscious, He spoke the two verses beginning with "Dvipādako yaṃ" (This two-footed one), wishing to censure heedlessness (pamāda) which causes obstacles to such great benefits, through a brief teaching. In those verses, although the bodies of footless creatures and others are also impure, He said "This two-footed one" by way of the context of this teaching, or by way of defining the superior human being. Or, because other impure bodies can be processed with salt, sourness, and so forth and brought as food for humans, whereas the human body cannot be so brought; therefore, even to show its state of being more impure, He said "Two-footed one."

By the word "ayaṃ" (this), He shows the human body. "Dugganḍho parihīrati" means that although it has a foul smell, it is carried about after being specially prepared with the scent of flowers and the like. "Nānākuṇapaparipūro" means it is full of various kinds of impurities such as hair and so forth. "Vissavanto tato tato" means that although they strive to cover it with the scent of flowers and the like, making that effort fruitless, saliva, snot, and so forth constantly flow from the nine openings, and sweat and grime constantly exude from the pores of the skin. Now, behold in that foulness! With such a body, some foolish man or woman might think to be conceited. Through craving, wrong view, and pride, one might think to be conceited in such ways as "I," "Mine," or "Permanent." Placing oneself in a high position, one might despise others based on birth and so forth. Apart from the lack of seeing the Noble Truths through the Noble Path, what other cause could there be for such conceit and contempt in that person?

At the conclusion of the teaching, the bhikkhunī named Nandā, the Beauty of the Country (Janapadakalyāṇī), attained spiritual urgency (saṃvega). She thought, "O, alas! I have been foolish indeed, that I did not come to attend upon the Blessed One who has promoted such various Dhamma teachings prompted by me alone." Having thus gained spiritual urgency, she [listened] to that very Dhamma teaching...
244:
Having reflected well on that Dhamma teaching, he realized the fruit of Arahantship within a few days through that very meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna). On the second occasion, at the end of the Dhamma teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma; the celestial maiden Sirimā attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and that monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

## The explanation of the Vijaya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā is finished.

## 12. Munisuttavaṇṇanā
"Santhavāto bhayaṃ jātaṃ" (From intimacy, fear is born) and so on is the Muni Sutta. How did it arise? Not all suttas have only one origin; however, the origin of the first four verses of this Muni Sutta is as follows: While the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, a certain poor woman living in a village, whose husband had died, had her son ordained among the monks and she herself ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Both of them, having entered the vassa (rains retreat) in Sāvatthī, constantly desired to see each other. When the mother received even a small gain, she would bring it to her son; the son also did the same for his mother. Thus, meeting each other in the evening and the morning, sharing whatever gains they received, rejoicing together, and asking about each other's well-being and suffering, they lived without suspicion.

Due to such frequent meetings, intimacy arose; from intimacy came familiarity; from familiarity came an opening (for lust). For those whose minds were overcome by lust, the perception of being ordained and the perception of being mother and son disappeared. Therefore, having transgressed the boundaries (of discipline), they engaged in misconduct (asaddhamma). Having fallen into disgrace, they disrobed and lived in the household life. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One rebuked them, saying, "Monks, does that foolish man think that a mother does not feel lust for her son, or a son for his mother?" Then, having stirred the monks with the rest of the sutta beginning with "Monks, I do not see any other single form..." (A. Ni. 5.55), He said: "Therefore, monks—

'Like the deadly Halāhala poison, like boiling oil, like molten copper, one should avoid women.'"
245:
Having said this, the Blessed One, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the monks once again, spoke these four verses compared to himself, beginning with "Santhavāto bhayaṃ jātaṃ" (Fear arises from intimacy). Therein, "Santhava" (intimacy) was previously mentioned as being of three kinds: craving, views, and friends. Here, however, intimacy of craving and intimacy of views are intended. Referring to that intimacy, the Blessed One said: "Monks, look at how this fear has arisen for that worthless man because of intimacy." Indeed, for him, because of the craving such as the desire to constantly see his mother, a powerful fear of defilements arose, by which, being unable to restrain himself, he acted wrongly towards his mother. Or, it refers to the great fear such as self-reproach, by which he abandoned the Dispensation and disrobed. "Niketa" (abode/attachment) refers to the various types of sense objects, as taught in the manner: "Householder, one who is attached to and bound by the signs of forms is called 'one who dwells in an abode'" (S.N. 3.3). "Jāyate rajo" means the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion is born. What is meant? Not only did fear arise for him from intimacy, but also, from that which is called "Niketa"—the objects of the taints (āsava) because they are the dwelling place of defilements—now, because of his broken restraint and his transgression of boundaries, dust arises even more from that Niketa. Because of that dust, with a defiled mind, he will reach ruin and destruction. Alternatively, "Monks, look at how this fear arose for that worthless man because of intimacy, and how dust is born from the abode (niketa) for all worldlings"—thus these two phrases should be connected.

In every way, by the first half of this verse, the Blessed One, having censured the view of worldlings and wishing to praise his own view, spoke the latter half beginning with "Aniketaṃ" (homeless/unattached). Therein, "Aniketa" is known by the rejection of the aforementioned Niketa, and "Asanthava" by the rejection of Santhava. Both of these are synonyms for Nibbāna. "Etaṃ ve munidassanaṃ" means that this Nibbāna, which is without the abode of craving and without intimacy, has been seen by the Sage (Muni), the Buddha. Therein, the word "ve" is to be understood as a particle in the sense of wonder. Therefore, the meaning is established: "While even mother and son act wrongly through the power of abode and intimacy, this state of being without abode and without intimacy has been seen by the Sage—oh, how wonderful!" Alternatively, "Muni-dassana" means the view of the Sage; "Dassana" means patience (khanti) and preference (ruci), meaning the Sage likes and desires that Nibbāna. In the second verse, "Yo jātamucchijjā" means as one abandons the defilement that has arisen, been produced, or generated in any object, just as one abandons an arisen unwholesome state...
246: A person making such an effort cuts off the defilements (kilesas) at the root so they do not arise again in that object. Because future defilements are imminent and ready to arise if such supporting conditions meet, they are called 'arising' (jāyanta) by way of the present characteristic close to the present; one should not plant them. This means that just as one strives so that unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, one should not let those defilements be produced. How should one not let them be produced? One should not let them enter continuously. One should not let the cause by which those defilements might arise enter or combine. Thus, by making the supporting factors deficient, one should not plant that which is arising. Alternatively, because of the development of the Path (magga-bhāvanā), past defilements are cut off as they no longer produce results in the future. Present defilements are not planted as they no longer enter. Future defilements cannot enter the mental continuum because the capacity for their arising has been destroyed. Therefore, one who cuts off what has arisen through the development of the Noble Path and does not plant what is arising, and does not let future arising defilements enter—such a person wandering alone is called a 'Muni.' That Mahesī (the Great Sage who seeks virtues) has seen the state of peace, Nibbāna. This is how the connection of meaning should be understood here. He is called 'Eka' (One/Alone) because of being absolutely free from defilements, or 'Eka' in the sense of being noble. 'Muninaṃ' means the Muni, or the noble one among Munis. 'Carantaṃ' means one who wanders with the practice for the benefit of the world, which is complete in every aspect, and with other practices. 'Addakkhi' means he saw. 'So' (He) refers to the Buddha-Muni who was spoken of as 'one should not plant what is arising, one should not let it enter' because of his ability to cut off what has arisen, not plant it, and not let it enter. 'Santipadaṃ' means the portion of peace. Among the three types of peace—conventional peace (sammuti-santi), temporary peace (tadaṅga-santi), and ultimate peace (accanta-santi) found in the divisions of the sixty-two views, insight, and Nibbāna—the Mahesī saw the ultimate peace, which is the most noble, in this unpeaceful world. This is how the meaning should be understood. In the third verse, 'saṅkhāya' means having calculated and delimited, having investigated and reflected, having known according to reality, and having fully understood through the full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā). 'Vatthūni' refers to the bases of defilements consisting of the aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) to which the people of this world are attached. 'Pamāya bījaṃ' means having oppressed and harassed the seed of those bases, which is the karmic consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa), and having abandoned it through the abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). 'Sinehamassa nānuppavecche' means that the seed, which is moistened by the moisture of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi), could produce the aforementioned crop of bases through rebirth in the future; one should not let that moisture enter. This means one should not let that moisture enter through the development of the Path, which is the opposite of that moisture. 'Sa ve muni jātikhayantadassī' means that such a Buddha-Muni has seen Nibbāna, which is the end of birth and death, through the realization of Nibbāna.
247:
That Buddha, the seer of Nibbāna which is the end of the destruction of birth, having abandoned speculative thought (takka), no longer falls into the reckoning of a worldling (puthujjana). By developing these Four Truths, he abandons the ninefold unwholesome thoughts, reaches the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu), and while performing the practice for the benefit of the world, upon reaching the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) through the gradual cessation of the final consciousness, he no longer falls into the reckoning of 'being a deva' or 'being a human.' Alternatively, just as one who has not yet attained final Nibbāna falls into the reckoning of 'this person is lustful' or 'this person is hateful' because of not having abandoned thoughts such as sensual thoughts, so too, having abandoned speculative thought, he no longer falls into reckoning. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

In the fourth verse, 'aññāya' means having known through methods such as impermanence (anicca). 'Sabbāni' means all without exception. 'Nivesanāni' refers to existences such as the sensual existence (kāma-bhava). Because beings dwell in those existences, they are called 'nivesanāni' (dwellings). Not longing for even a single one of those existences, such a Buddha-Muni, who sees the danger in views and so forth, is called 'vītagadha' (free from greed) because greed, which is craving, has vanished through the power of developing the Path. Because he is free from greed, he is 'agiddha' (not greedy). It is not like some who, while not yet free from greed, claim 'we are not greedy.' 'Nāyūhati' means he no longer performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds that produce those respective dwellings (existences). Why? Because he has reached the other shore, Nibbāna. This means such a person has reached Nibbāna, which is the end of all dwellings of existence.

Thus, with the first verse, he censures the views of worldlings and praises his own view. With the second verse, he praises his own attainment of the state of peace because of the absence of those defilements by which a worldling is unpeaceful. With the third verse, he praises his own non-entry into reckoning by abandoning speculative thought through the development of the Four Truths regarding those bases where a worldling, without abandoning speculative thought, falls into various reckonings. With the fourth verse, he praises his own non-striving because of the absence of craving for those dwellings (existences) for which a worldling, longing for them in the future, strives through craving for existence. With these four verses, placing Arahantship at the summit, he concluded the teaching which has a single theme.

## How did the topic 'Sabbābhibhū' arise?
The Great Man (Mahāpurisa), having made the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana), gradually attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and went to Vārāṇasī to preach the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta...
248:
A person of such a nature reaches Nibbāna, which is the further shore of the houses of all existences. This is the meaning. Thus, having censured the view of the worldling with the first verse, He spoke the second verse wishing to praise His own view. Wishing to praise Nibbāna, the means of reaching His own peace due to the absence of those defilements by which a worldling is made restless, He spoke the third verse. Wishing to praise the state of not falling into the category of a worldling by abandoning sensual thoughts and the like through the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths—in those objects where a worldling, without abandoning sensual thoughts and the like, falls into the category of a worldling in various ways—He spoke the fourth verse. Wishing to praise His own lack of striving, as a worldling who longs for the houses of future existences strives with the craving for existence, He concluded the teaching, which has a single origin, by placing the Fruit of Arahantship at the pinnacle with these four verses.

What is the origin of this verse beginning with 'Sabbābhibhū'? The Buddha, the Great Man, having made the Great Renunciation and gradually attained Omniscience, was traveling to Bārāṇasī to preach the Dhammacakka sermon when He met an Ājīvaka named Upaka between the Bodhi-maṇḍa and Gayā. That Upaka questioned Him in this manner: 'Friend, your faculties are very serene,' and so on. The Blessed One replied with the words, 'I am the All-Conqueror,' and so forth. Upaka said, 'It may be so, friend,' shook his head, took a side path, and departed. Traveling by stages, he reached a certain hunter's village in the Vaṅgahāra country. When the hunter chief saw Upaka, he thought, 'How wonderful! This ascetic has few desires; he does not even wear clothes. This man must be an Arahant in the world.' He took him home, served him with meat broth, and after he had eaten, the hunter, along with his wife and children, paid homage and invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please reside right here; I will support you with the four requisites.' He then prepared a dwelling place for him. Upaka resided there.

In the summer, when the deer departed for a cool place abundant with water, the hunter, as he was preparing to go there, commanded his daughter named Chāpā, 'Attend to our venerable Arahant with respect,' and then departed with his sons and brothers. That daughter was beautiful and possessed perfect limbs. On the second day, when Upaka came to the house and saw the young woman approaching to perform her duties and serve him, he was overcome by lust. Unable even to eat, he took the rice in a bowl, went to his dwelling, set the food aside in a place, and lay down without eating, thinking, 'If I get Chāpā, I shall live; if not, I shall die.' On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter about Upaka. She said, 'He came only on the first day and has not returned since.' The hunter thought, 'I will approach and question him just as I have arrived,' and went immediately. Massaging Upaka's feet, he asked, 'Venerable sir, what is your ailment?' Upaka just rolled from side to side, groaning. The hunter said, 'Speak, venerable sir; whatever I can do, I will do it all.' Upaka said, 'If I get Chāpā, I shall live; if not, death right here is better.' The hunter asked, 'But do you know any craft, venerable sir?' 'I do not,' he replied. 'Venerable sir, one who knows no craft cannot maintain a household,' the hunter said. Upaka replied, 'I know no craft, but I will be a meat-carrier for you and I will sell the meat.' The hunter agreed, saying, 'This work is suitable for us,' gave him an upper garment, took him home, and gave him his daughter in marriage. As they lived together...
249:
A son was born. They named the boy Subhadda. Cāpā teased Upaka with a song to soothe the child. Unable to endure that teasing, Upaka said, "Lady, I am going to the presence of the Anantajina (Infinite Victor)," and set out towards the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa).

At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Great Monastery in Sāvatthī. Then the Blessed One pre-emptively instructed the monks: "Monks, if anyone comes asking for the Anantajina, show me to him."

Upaka eventually arrived at Sāvatthī, stood in the middle of the monastery, and asked, "In this monastery, there is my friend named Anantajina; where does he live?" The monks led Upaka to the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught him a suitable Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, he was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). The monks, having heard of Upaka's past events, started a discussion: "The Blessed One first taught the Dhamma to a luckless naked ascetic." The Blessed One, knowing the topic of their conversation, came out from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), sat on the Buddha's seat with a psychic power suitable for the moment, and addressed the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" They told him everything. Then the Blessed One said: "Monks, the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma without cause or condition. The Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma is stainless; no fault can be seen therein. Monks, by depending on that Dhamma teaching, Upaka has now become a Non-returner." Having said this, he uttered this verse illustrating the stainless nature of his teaching.

The meaning of that verse is: Because he is not overcome by all the aggregates, sense bases, and elements which are objects of the taints (āsava) through the abandoning of desire and lust, and because he himself exists having overcome all those things, he is called 'Conqueror of All' (Sabbābhibhū). Because he has known those things and all other things in every aspect, he is called 'All-knower' (Sabbavidū). Because he is endowed with the beautiful wisdom called 'medhā' which is capable of teaching all Dhammas, he is called 'One of Good Wisdom' (Sumedha). By whatever smears of craving and views one is smeared in all things such as the aggregates accompanied by taints, because those smears do not exist, he is 'Unstained' (Anupalitta) in all those things. Because he stands having abandoned all those things through the absence of desire and lust, he is 'Abandoner of All' (Sabbañjaha). Because he is specially liberated in Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, with a mind inclined towards seclusion from the substrates (upadhi), he is called 'Liberated in the Destruction of Craving' (Taṇhakkhaye vimutta); this also means 'Adhimutta' (intent on). The wise also know such a person as a Sage (Muni). Behold how extraordinary this Sage is; where could there be any stain in his teaching? Thus he showed himself.
250:
In this word, the particle 'vā' clarifies the meaning. Some teachers, however, explain: "At that time, even though Upaka saw the Tathāgata, he did not believe 'This is the Buddha-Sage.'" How did the monks raise this matter? Then the Blessed One, wishing to show "Whether Upaka believes or not, the wise know that Sage," uttered this verse.

What is the origin of the verse 'Paññābalaṃ'? This verse was spoken concerning the Elder Revata. In the same manner as stated in the verse "Gāme vā yadi vā raññe", one should understand the Elder Revata's ordination from the beginning, his dwelling in the Acacia forest (Khadiravana) after ordaining, his attainment of distinction while living there, and the Blessed One's journey there and back. When the Blessed One returned, an elderly monk who had forgotten his sandals went back and saw them hanging on an Acacia tree. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, when the laywoman Visākhā asked the monks, "Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of the Elder Revata pleasant?", that monk, wishing to discourage her from the praise of other monks, said, "Laywoman, those monks speak in vain; that ground is not good, it is merely a very parched and rough Acacia forest." After eating the meal for guests provided by Visākhā, in the afternoon when the monks were assembled in the pavilion, he said, wishing to disparage them, "Friends, what did you see that was pleasant in the Elder Revata's monastery?" The Blessed One, knowing that talk, came out from the Fragrant Chamber, reached the midst of the assembly with a psychic power suitable for the moment, sat on the Buddha's seat, and addressed the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, a discussion has arisen concerning Revata: 'When will one who is thus occupied with new work (navakammika) practice the recluse's Dhamma?'" "Monks, Revata is not one occupied with new work; Revata is an Arahant whose taints are destroyed." Having said this, he uttered this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.

The meaning of that verse is: Because he is endowed with the power of wisdom that accomplishes the abandoning of the weak defilements, or with the power of wisdom consisting of various psychic transformations (vikubbana) and resolutions (adhiṭṭhāna), he is called 'Power of Wisdom' (Paññābala). Because he is endowed with the fourfold purification of virtue and the ascetic practices (dhutanga), he is called 'Endowed with Virtue and Vows' (Sīlavatūpapanna). Because he is composed through the concentration of the path, the concentration of fruition, and the concentration of postures, he is called 'Concentrated' (Samāhita). Because he delights in Jhana, whether by way of access and absorption or simply delighting in meditation, he is called 'Delighting in Jhana' (Jhānaraata). Because he has reached abundance of mindfulness, he is called 'Mindful' (Satimaṃ). Because he is released from bonds such as lust, he is called 'Freed from Bonds' (Saṅgāpamutta). Because of the absence of the five mental wildernesses (cetokhila) and the four taints (āsava), he is called 'Free from Wilderness' (Akhila) and 'Taintless' (Anāsava). The wise know such a person as a Sage. The wise beings know such a person, who is endowed with qualities like wisdom and disconnected from faults like bonds, as a Sage. Behold to what extent...
251:
This monk, whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), is exceedingly excellent. How could such a person be called 'one engaged in new work' (navakammika) or be asked 'when will he perform the monk's practice?' Indeed, he completed that monastery through the power of wisdom, not by performing physical construction. He has already done what was to be done (katakicco); he no longer needs to perform the monk's practice. Thus, the Buddha clarified the status of Elder Revata. Here, the word 'vā' has the sense of clarification.

What is the origin of the verse beginning with 'Ekaṃ carantaṃ'? After the Blessed One reached Kapilavatthu in due order from the Bodhi tree, during the reunion of father and son, King Suddhodana, being delighted, addressed him: 'Venerable Sir, when you were a householder, you wore cloths from the Kāsī country scented with perfume boxes; why do you now wear these cut-up rag-robes (paṃsukūla)?' and so forth. The Blessed One, wishing to persuade the King, said:

'O Father, you speak to me of the silk, fine linen, and Kāsī cloth. Rag-robes are more excellent than those; that is what I have desired.'

Having spoken these and other words, and demonstrating his unshakable nature amidst the worldly conditions (lokadhamma), the Buddha preached this seven-line verse for the benefit of the King's Dhamma instruction.

The meaning of that verse is: 'Ekaṃ carantaṃ' means wandering alone through renunciation and so forth, and through the practices of the postures. He is called a 'muni' (sage) because he is endowed with the qualities of a sage (moneyya-dhamma). He is 'appamatta' (heedful) because of the absence of negligence in all places. He is one who does not tremble (avedhamāna) through the power of aversion or favor towards blame (nindā), such as abuse and reproach, or towards praise (pasaṃsā), such as commendation and glorification. It should be understood that through the mention of blame and praise, all eight worldly conditions are included here. Like a lion among sounds such as the roar of a drum, he is 'asantasanta' (not startled) because he does not undergo any change from his natural state amidst the eight worldly conditions; or, he is without fear in secluded lodgings. Like the wind in a net made of thread and so forth, he is 'asajjamāna' (not clinging) to the net of craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi) through the four paths; or, he does not cling to the eight worldly conditions through aversion or favor. Like a lotus in water, although born in the world, he is 'alippamāna' (not smeared) by the world because he has abandoned those stains of craving and views by which beings are smeared in the world. Having produced the path leading to Nibbāna, he is the leader of other devas and humans by that path. However, because he himself does not need to be led by anyone else showing the path, he is 'ananyaneyya' (not to be led by others). The wise know him as a 'muni'; they know him as a 'Buddha-muni'. Thus, the Buddha clarified his own nature. The remaining meanings are just as previously explained.
252:
What is the origin (uppatti) of the verse beginning with 'Yo ogahaṇe'? The Blessed One fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), the secondary perfections (upapāramīs), and the ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramīs) in their ten-fold divisions, along with the perfections of the quality of aspiration (abhinīhāra-guṇa-pāramī), for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. He possessed the quality of being reborn in the Tusita heaven, the quality of residing there, the quality of the five great observations, the descent into the mother's womb, the stay in the womb, the birth from the womb, the taking of seven steps, the surveying of the directions, the lion's roar like a Brahma, the great renunciation, the great effort, the supreme enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dhamma, the four-fold path-knowledge and fruition-knowledge, the knowledge of being unshakable in the eight assemblies, the ten powers (dasabala-ñāṇa), the knowledge of defining the four modes of birth, the knowledge of defining the five destinations, the six-fold uncommon knowledge, the eight-fold Buddha-knowledge common to disciples, the fourteen-fold Buddha-knowledge, the knowledge of defining the eighteen Buddha-qualities, the nineteen-fold reviewing knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. Relying on these hundreds of thousands of qualities, great gain and honor arose for him. Unable to endure this, the heretics (titthiyas) instigated Ciñca Māṇavikā who, as told in the story of the verse 'Ekaṃ dhammaṃ atītassa', created disrepute (slander) against the Blessed One in the midst of the four-fold assembly. Because of that, the monks started a conversation: 'Even when such disrepute has arisen, there is no change in the Blessed One's mind!' Knowing this, the Blessed One emerged from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), reached the midst of the assembly through a miracle suitable for that moment, sat on the Buddha's seat, and addressed the monks: 'Monks, for what discussion are you sitting here now?' They told him everything. Then the Blessed One said: 'Monks, Buddhas are such (tādi) amidst the eight worldly conditions,' and he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.

The meaning of that verse is: Just as people at a bathing place (ogahaṇe) rub their limbs against a four-sided or eight-sided pillar (thambha) erected for that purpose, whether they are of high birth or low birth, there is no rising or sinking of that pillar. In the same way, he who is like a pillar at a bathing place remains firm when others (heretics or others) speak words that reach the limit—either superior words by way of praise or inferior words by way of blame. What is meant? In whatever matter others speak words to the limit, either high through praise or low through blame, he does not fall into favor or aversion, and by being 'such' (tādi), he is like a pillar at a bathing place. He is called 'vītarāga' (free from lust) because of the absence of lust for pleasant objects, and 'susamāhitindriya' (one with well-composed senses) because of the absence of hatred and delusion towards unpleasant objects, or because his senses are well-collected and well-guarded.
253:
It means one who has guarded faculties. Wise ones know such a person as a Muni; they know him as a Buddha-Muni. He revealed himself, [thinking], "How could the mind of such a Buddha-Muni be otherwise (disturbed)?" The rest is just as previously explained.

What is the origin of the verse beginning with 'Yo ve thitatto'? It is said that in the city of Sāvatthī, a certain daughter of a merchant descended from her mansion and went to the weavers' shed below the mansion. Seeing them winding the shuttle (tasara), she took the straightness of that shuttle as an object of reflection, thinking, "Oh, may all beings abandon the crookedness of body, speech, and mind, and have straight minds like a shuttle."

Even after ascending back to her mansion, she remained seated, repeatedly reflecting on that same sign. As she practiced in this way, before long, the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) became clear to her, and by following that, the marks of suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta) also became clear. Then, the three realms of existence appeared to her as if they were ablaze. Knowing that she was thus practicing insight (vipassanā), the Blessed One, while seated in the Gandhakuti, radiated light. Seeing that light and wondering, "What is this?", she saw the Blessed One as if he were sitting by her side; she stood up and remained with palms joined in respect. Then, the Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for her, spoke this verse by way of Dhamma teaching.

The meaning of that verse is: A person is 'steadfast' (thitatto) because of the one-pointedness of mind, because of the unshakable liberation (akuppa-vimutti), because of the absence of growth and decay, because of having exhausted the cycle of rebirth, and because of the absence of going to another existence. He is 'straight like a shuttle' (tasaraṃva uju) because of having abandoned the crookedness of body, speech, and mind, or because of not following the wrong paths (agati). Because he is endowed with moral shame and dread (hiri-ottappa), he 'loathes' (jigucchati) evil deeds. It means he loathes and is ashamed of evil deeds just as one loathes excrement or urine. In the science of grammar, by the method of Yoga-vibhāga, the third case (instrumental) is established in the sense of the second case (accusative).

'Vīmaṃsamāno visamaṃ samañca' means one who investigates and examines with path-wisdom (magga-paññā), accomplishing the task of abandoning the unevenness (visama) such as bodily misconduct and developing the evenness (sama) such as bodily good conduct. Wise ones know such an Arahant as a Muni. What is meant? One who investigates with path-wisdom according to the stated method and knows the uneven and the even, and who is indeed steadfast; such a person, being straight like a shuttle and not falling into even the slightest transgression, loathes evil deeds. Wise ones know him as a Muni. To show that such a person is an Arahant-Muni, the Buddha taught the verse, crowning it with the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). At the conclusion of the teaching, the merchant's daughter—
254:
—was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). In this context, the word 'vā' should be understood in the sense of either distinction (vikappa) or conjunction (samuccaya).

What is the origin of the words 'Yo saññatatto'? It is said that while the Blessed One was staying in Āḷavī, a certain weaver in the city of Āḷavī commanded his seven-year-old daughter: "Dear daughter, there is not much of yesterday's remaining shuttle-thread; spin the shuttle quickly and come to the weaving shed; do not be long." She accepted, saying, "Very well." The father went to the shed and stood there weaving.

On that day, the Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) and surveying the world, saw the girl's supporting condition (upanissaya) for the fruit of Stream-entry, and also saw that eighty-four thousand beings would realize the Dhamma at the end of the teaching. Early in the morning, after attending to his physical needs, he took his bowl and robes and entered the city. When the people saw the Blessed One, they approached him, saying, "Surely today there is someone to be favored; the Blessed One has entered the city very early."

The Blessed One stood on the path by which the girl would go to her father. The city dwellers swept that place, sprinkled water, made offerings of flowers, hung a canopy, and prepared a seat. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat, and a great crowd of people stood surrounding him. When the girl reached that place and saw the Blessed One surrounded by the great crowd, she paid homage with the fivefold prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita). The Blessed One addressed her and asked, "Girl, where have you come from?"

"I do not know, Blessed One," she replied.
"Where will you go?"
"I do not know, Blessed One."
"Do you not know?"
"I know, Blessed One."
"Do you know?"
"I do not know, Blessed One."

Hearing this, the people complained: "Look, sirs, this girl says 'I do not know' when asked by the Blessed One even though she came from her own house. She says 'I do not know' even though she is going to the weaving shed. When asked 'Do you not know?', she says 'I know', and when asked 'Do you know?', she says 'I do not know'. She is doing everything in contradiction!"

The Blessed One, wishing to make the matter clear to the people, asked her: "What did I ask, and what did you say?" She said: "Venerable Sir, there is no one who does not know that I have come from home and am going to the weaving shed. However, you asked me by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi), 'Where have you come from?', and you asked me by way of death (cuti), 'Where will you go?'. And I do not know. I do not know from where I have come, whether from hell or the deva world. Likewise, I do not know where I will go, whether to hell or the deva world. Therefore, I replied 'I do not know'." Therefore...
255: I replied, 'I know.' Then the Blessed One, referring to death, asked, 'Do you not know?' and I knew. Because I knew that 'the death of all beings is certain,' I replied, 'I know.' Then the Blessed One, referring to the time of death, asked, 'Do you know?' and I did not know. Because I did not know 'when I shall die, whether today or tomorrow,' I replied, 'I do not know.' The Blessed One, expressing approval of the answer given by the girl, said, 'Excellent, excellent!' The multitude also gave thousands of cheers, saying, 'How exceedingly wise is this girl!' Then the Blessed One, knowing the Dhamma that was suitable for the young girl's effort and wishing to preach the Dhamma, spoke this verse: ## 'Blind is this world; few here see with insight. Like a bird escaped from a net, few go to heaven.' At the end of the verse, the girl was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), and eighty-four thousand beings also attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). Having paid homage to the Blessed One, she went to her father. When the father saw her, he became angry, saying, 'Have you come only after so long?' and threw the weaver's shuttle (vema) with force. The shuttle flew out from the loom and pierced the girl's belly. She passed away (cuti) right there. Seeing this, the father thought, 'I did not strike my daughter; rather, this shuttle flew out with force and pierced her belly. Is she still alive or not?' Upon investigating and seeing her dead, he thought, 'If people know that "this man has killed his daughter," they will reproach me; for that reason, the King will also impose a heavy punishment. I shall flee immediately.' Fearing punishment, he fled and, having taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence of the Blessed One, reached the dwelling place of the monks living in the forest. Approaching those monks, he requested ordination. The monks ordained him and gave him the meditation on the fivefold skin-parts (taca-pañcaka kammaṭṭhāna). Having learned that meditation and striving, he attained the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) before long. Those monks were his teachers and preceptors. Then, at the Great Pavāraṇā festival, all the monks went to the presence of the Blessed One, saying, 'We shall perform the Pavāraṇā of Purity (visuddhi-pavāraṇā).' After performing the Pavāraṇā and completing the rainy season retreat, the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, wandered through villages and towns, eventually reaching the city of Āḷavī. There, when the people invited the Blessed One and performed acts of merit such as giving alms, they saw that monk and mocked him, saying, 'Having killed your daughter, for whom have you come to kill now?' and so on. The monks, hearing those words, approached the Blessed One at the time of attending to him and reported the matter. The Blessed One said, 'Monks, it is not so...'
256: 'Monks, this monk did not kill his daughter; she died due to her own kamma.' Having said this, wishing to reveal the monk's state as an Arahant sage (khīṇāsava-muni), which is difficult for people to know, and for the benefit of preaching the Dhamma to the monks, he spoke this verse. The meaning of that verse is: The monk who is restrained in his person through the restraint of virtue in the three doors of action (kamma-dvāra) does no evil such as harming others by way of body, speech, or mind. He never does such evil, whether he be one established in youth, in middle age, or in the same way, in the final stage of life (as an elder). For what reason? Because he is one whose person is restrained. It means his mind is far removed from all evil through supreme renunciation. Now, regarding the words 'The sage is unassailable; he does not provoke anyone,' the grammatical connection and meaning are: That Arahant sage is unassailable; he should not be provoked, struck, or harassed by way of body or speech with such words as 'daughter-killer' or 'weaver.' He also does not provoke anyone; he does not provoke, strike, or harass anyone by saying words such as 'I did not kill my daughter; you killed her, or someone like you killed her.' Therefore, he too is unassailable. Indeed, he should only be worshipped with humble respect in the manner stated: 'Let the great elephant (nāga) be; do not strike the elephant; pay homage to the elephant.' In the phrase 'taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayanti,' the word-division should be understood as 'the wise also know such a monk as a sage.' The meaning here is: Foolish people, not knowing that 'this person is unassailable,' provoke that sage. But those who are wise, they alone know that sage, recognizing that 'this monk is an Arahant sage.' The occasion for the verse beginning with 'yadaggato' is as follows: In the city of Sāvatthī, there was a brahmin named Pañcaggadāyaka. When the crops were ripe, that brahmin used to give these five kinds of first-fruits (agga): the first-fruits of the field, the first-fruits of the heap, the first-fruits of the granary, the first-fruits of the pot, and the first-fruits of the meal. Among those five kinds of first-fruits, he would have the ears of the first-ripened rice, barley, and wheat brought, and having prepared gruel, milk-rice, parched rice, and so on, he held the view that 'the wise person who gives the first-fruits obtains the best.' Thus, to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha...
257: That Brahmin was one who gave offerings; this offering was his first-fruits of the field (khettagga-dāna). When the paddy crops were fully grown, harvested, and threshed, he would take the excellent grains and give an offering in the same manner; this was his first-fruits of the heap (rāsagga-dāna). Again, having filled the granaries with those grains, when first opening a granary, he would take the grains first removed and give an offering in the same manner; this was his first-fruits of the granary (koṭṭhagga-dāna). Whatever rice was cooked in the house, he would not give anything even to children, let alone to monks who arrived, without first giving the first portion; this was his first-fruits of the pot (kumbhi-agga-dāna). Again, at his own mealtime, he would not eat without giving the first-served food to the Saṅgha in the morning, or to beggars who arrived in the afternoon, or in their absence, even to dogs; this was his first-fruits of the meal (bhojanagga-dāna). In this way, that Brahmin became known as the 'Pañcaggadāyaka' (Giver of Five First-fruits). Then one day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) in that Brahmin and his wife. Having performed his bodily ablutions, he entered the Gandhakuṭi very early. The monks, seeing the Gandhakuṭi with its doors closed, understood, 'Today the Blessed One wishes to enter the village alone,' and at the time for alms-round, they circumambulated the Gandhakuṭi and entered for alms. The Blessed One also set out at the Brahmin's mealtime and entered the city of Sāvatthī. People, seeing the Blessed One, thought, 'Today there must be some being to be graced, for the Blessed One has entered alone,' and they did not approach the Blessed One to invite him. The Blessed One, in due course, reached the door of the Brahmin's house and stood there. At that time, the Brahmin was seated holding his food, while the Brahmin woman stood holding a fan. Seeing the Blessed One, she thought, 'If this Brahmin sees him, he will take the bowl and give all the food; then I will have to cook again.' Thus, giving rise to a lack of faith and to stinginess, she hid the Blessed One with the fan so that the Brahmin would not see him. The Blessed One, knowing this, emitted a radiance from his body. The Brahmin, seeing that golden light, looked up wondering 'What is this?' and saw the Blessed One standing at the door. The Brahmin woman, realizing 'He has seen the Blessed One,' immediately put down the fan, approached the Blessed One, and paid homage with the five-point prostration. When she rose from her homage, the Blessed One, knowing the suitable opportunity, said: 'He who has no sense of "mine" in name and form in every way, and who does not grieve for what is not, he is truly called a bhikkhu.' (Dhp. 367)
258: He spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, the Brahmin woman was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). The Brahmin also invited the Blessed One into the house, had him sit on a noble seat, offered the water of dedication, and presented the food prepared for himself. He said, 'Venerable Sir, you are the supreme recipient of offerings in the world including the devas. Please, accept this food of mine in your bowl.' The Blessed One, to show him grace, accepted and partook of it. When the meal was finished, knowing the Brahmin's inclination, he spoke this verse. The meaning of that verse is: One may receive alms from the top, because it is taken first from the pot; or from the middle, because it is taken from the pot when half remains; or from the remainder, because it is taken from the pot when only one or two ladles remain. A monk is one who lives on what is given by others (paradattūpajīvī). Indeed, except for water and the tooth-stick, he lives depending on everything else given by others; therefore, he is called 'one who lives on what is given by others.' Even if he receives the best (excellent alms), he should not praise himself or the donor, because he has abandoned attachment (anunaya). Even if he receives the remainder (poor alms), he is not one who speaks unpleasant words by disparaging the donor, saying 'Why did this person give such leftovers?', because he has abandoned resentment (paṭigha). The wise know such a person, who has abandoned attachment and resentment, as a 'Muni' (Sage). Thus, the Blessed One preached the verse to the Brahmin, culminating in the Fruit of Arahantship. At the end of the verse, the Brahmin was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. How did the verse beginning with 'Muniṃ carantaṃ' arise? It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain son of a merchant, while enjoying all kinds of prosperity in three palaces according to the seasons, desired to ordain even while young. Having asked his parents, as described in the origin of the verse 'Kāmā hi citrā' in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, he ordained and disrobed three times, and on the fourth time, he attained Arahantship. Because of their previous familiarity, the monks said to him, 'Friend, it is time to disrobe.' He replied, 'Friends, I am now incapable of disrobing.' Hearing this, the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, 'Monks, it is so; he is now incapable of disrobing,' and revealing his status as a Muni whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), he spoke this verse.
259:
The meaning of that verse is: One is called a 'Muni' (sage) because of being endowed with the qualities of a sage (moneyya-dhamma). It refers to one who lives alone, practicing any of the previously mentioned practices, and who, unlike before, does not incline the mind toward carnal practice (methuna-dhamma), but refrains from it through supreme abstinence. The connection of the second foot of the verse is: What kind of sage is it who, while practicing, refrains from carnal practice? It is one who, in the prime of youth, has no attachment to anyone; even when in the bloom of youth, he is not bound by carnal lust for the beauty of women as he was before. Alternatively, it means one who is not bound by lust, thinking either of his own youth or another's youth, 'I am still young,' or 'This person is young, so I will enjoy sensual pleasures for now.' This is the meaning here. Not only does he refrain from carnal practice, but indeed he also refrains from intoxications (mada) such as the pride of birth, and from negligence (pamāda) characterized by the loss of mindfulness regarding sensual pleasures. Thus, by refraining from intoxication and negligence, he is liberated from all fetters of defilements. It does not mean refraining like one who refrains through mundane abstinence (lokiya-virati); rather, it means one who is liberated from all fetters of defilements and refrains through supramundane abstinence (lokuttara-virati). 'The wise know him as a sage' (taṃ vāpi dhīရာ muni vedayanti) means that only the wise recognize such a person as a sage; you, however, do not know him, and that is why you speak of him in this way—this is what the Buddha shows.

What is the origin of the verse beginning with 'Aññāya lokaṃ'? The Blessed One was staying at Kapilavatthu. At that time, three auspicious ceremonies were being held for Prince Nanda: the ceremony of ornamentation, the ceremony of consecration, and the ceremony of marriage. The Blessed One, having been invited there, went with five hundred monks, and after taking his meal, he handed his bowl to Prince Nanda as he was departing. Seeing him depart, Princess Janapadakalyāṇī said, 'My Lord, please return quickly.' Out of respect for the Blessed One, Prince Nanda did not dare to say, 'Venerable Sir, please take the bowl,' and followed him all the way to the monastery. The Blessed One stood in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi and took the bowl, saying, 'Nanda, bring the bowl.' Then He asked, 'Will you ordain?' Out of great respect for the Blessed One, he did not dare to refuse and said, 'I will ordain, Bhante.' The Blessed One then ordained him. However, he remained dissatisfied in the Dispensation, repeatedly remembering the words of Janapadakalyāṇī. The monks informed the Blessed One. Wishing to dispel Nanda's dissatisfaction, the Blessed One asked, 'Nanda, have you ever been to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven?' Nanda replied, 'No, Bhante, I have never been there.' Then the Blessed One, by his psychic power, took him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and stood at the gate of the Vejayanta Palace. Knowing that the Blessed One had arrived, Sakka...
260:
Sakka descended from the palace surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs. All those nymphs had red feet like those of a dove because they had previously offered foot-wiping oil to the disciples of Kassapa Buddha. Then the Blessed One addressed Prince Nanda: 'Nanda, do you see these five hundred celestial nymphs with feet like those of a dove?' (In this way, the whole story should be expanded.) Such a statement as 'one should take hold of the signs and features of a woman's form' does not exist in the entirety of the Buddha's word. However, in this instance, the Blessed One, being highly skilled in means (upāyakusala), like a physician who makes a patient vomit out the humors to remove a disease, wished to make Nanda vomit out his lust. Therefore, He permitted the grasping of signs and features, in accordance with His attribute as the Incomparable Charioteer of men to be tamed (anuttaro purisadammasārathi).

Thereafter, the Blessed One, seeing Nanda's delight in the holy life for the sake of the nymphs, commanded the monks: 'Rebuke Nanda with the talk of him being a hireling.' Being rebuked by them, Nanda felt ashamed and, practicing with wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), he soon realized Arahantship. A deity living in a tree at the end of Nanda's walkway informed the Blessed One of this matter. Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One's mind. The monks, not knowing this, continued to rebuke the Venerable Nanda as before. The Blessed One said, 'Monks, Nanda should no longer be rebuked in this way.' To show that the Venerable Nanda was now a sage whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava-muni), He spoke this verse to teach those monks.

The meaning of that verse is: Having known and determined the world of the aggregates, etc., by defining the truth of suffering, and seeing the ultimate truth by realizing the truth of cessation; having crossed over the fourfold flood (ogha) by abandoning the truth of the origin (samudaya); and having crossed over the ocean of the sense bases (āyatana) such as the eye by enduring the impulses of the intoxication of form (rūpa-mada), etc., because the origin has been abandoned—having thus crossed over and transcended through the development of the Path, he is called 'Tādi' (the Steadfast) because he has reached the characteristic of 'Tādi' in accordance with the verse 'Tanniddesā tādī'. Alternatively, the mass of defilements such as sensual lust is called a 'flood' (ogha) in the sense of carrying away, and it is called an 'ocean' (samudda) in the sense of being difficult to fill due to the miserable destinations (gati). By abandoning the origin, he has crossed over that flood and ocean. Because he has fully crossed the flood, he is called 'Tādi' because he does not undergo any change even when you speak to him in this way—thus should the sense and meaning be understood. The words 'one whose bonds are cut, the independent, the taintless' are words of praise for that elder. He is called 'one whose bonds are cut' (chinnagantha) because the four bonds (gantha) have been cut through the development of the four truths. He is called 'independent' (asita) because he does not depend on anything through either wrong view or craving. He is called 'taintless' (anāsava) because of the absence of the four taints (āsava). 'The wise know him as a sage' means that only the wise recognize that sage whose taints are destroyed; you, however, do not know him and thus speak in this way—this is what the Buddha shows.
261:
What is the origin of the verse beginning with "Asamā ubho"? A certain monk was dwelling in the forest depending on a frontier village in the kingdom of Kosala. A hunter in that village used to go to the place where the monk resided to trap deer. When entering the forest, the hunter would see the Elder entering the village for alms, and when returning from the forest, he would see the Elder coming out of the village. Through such frequent sightings, he developed affection for the Elder. Whenever the hunter obtained plenty of meat, he would offer a delicious portion of alms-food to the Elder.

People began to criticize, saying, "This monk tells the hunter, 'Deer stay in such a place, they roam there, they drink water there.' Because of his words, the hunter kills the deer; thus, the two of them live in partnership."

Later, while the Blessed One was wandering through the countryside, he arrived at that region. The monks, hearing about this matter while entering the village for alms, reported it to the Blessed One. To prove that there was no shared livelihood with the hunter and to reveal the monk's status as a sage whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava muni), the Blessed One spoke this verse to teach those monks.

The meaning of that verse is: Monks, there is a monk and there is a hunter; these two are not the same. The statement made by people that "they have a shared livelihood" is false. For what reason? Because they are far apart in their dwelling and livelihood (dūravihāravuttino). Both their dwelling and their livelihood are far apart. "Vihāra" means the place of residence; for the monk, it is in the forest, and for the hunter, it is in the village. "Vutti" means livelihood; for the monk, it is the practice of begging for alms from house to house in the village, while for the hunter, it is the killing of deer and birds in the forest.

Furthermore, the hunter, being a layman, supports a wife and children; he maintains them through such deeds. The monk, whose taints are destroyed, is without possessiveness (amamo), being free from the sense of "mine" through craving and views regarding wife and children. He is called "subbata" (well-vowed) because of his pure and excellent practice. Furthermore, the hunter, as a layman, is unrestrained (asaññato) in harming other lives; being a layman, he is unrestrained in body, speech, and mind regarding the harming of others and the cutting off of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) of those beings. The other, the sage whose taints are destroyed, is always restrained (yato) in body, speech, and mind, and protects living beings. This being so, how could they possibly have a shared livelihood?

What is the origin of the verse beginning with "Sikhī yathā"? While the Blessed One was staying in Kapilavatthu, a discussion arose among the Sakyans: "One who became a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) first is superior in Dhamma to one who attained stream-entry later. Therefore, a monk who is a later stream-enterer should perform acts of respect, such as bowing, to a layman who was an earlier stream-enterer." That discussion...
262:
A certain monk who went for alms heard this and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, intending that "These grounds for worship (birth and appearance) are indeed distinct," said, "Monks, even if a layman is an Anāgāmī, he must still perform duties such as bowing to a novice (sāmaṇera) who was ordained on that very day." Then, wishing to show the great distinction of a monk who is a later stream-enterer over a layman who was an earlier stream-enterer, he spoke this verse to teach the monks.

The meaning of that verse should be understood as follows: The peacock is called a bird, known as "sikhī" because of the crest (sikhā) grown on its head, and "nīlagīvo" (blue-necked) because its neck resembles a jeweled staff. Just as among the varieties of green swans, ruddy swans, milk-white swans, black swans, grey swans, and golden swans, the peacock cannot match even a sixteenth part of the speed of the golden swan (suvaṇṇahaṃsa). For the golden swan can travel a thousand yojanas in a single moment, while the other, the peacock, cannot travel even one yojana. However, in terms of beauty, both are beautiful to look at. Similarly, a layman who is an earlier stream-enterer is indeed beautiful to behold through the vision of the Path. Nevertheless, he cannot match the speed of a monk who is a later stream-enterer, even though they are equal in the beauty of their vision of the Path. In what kind of speed can he not match him? He cannot match him in the speed of the insight knowledge of the higher paths (uparimagga-vipassanā-ñāṇa). For a layman, that knowledge is slow because it is entangled in the clutter of wife, children, and so on. For a monk, however, that knowledge is sharp and swift because he is free from such clutter. This meaning was shown by the Blessed One with the line: "The sage, secluded, meditating in the forest." This monk, a trainee sage (sekha-muni), is secluded through seclusion of body and mind, and always meditates in the forest through meditation on characteristics and objects (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). How could such seclusion and jhāna exist for a layman? This is the intention here.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Munisutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## The explanation of the first group, named the Uragavagga, is also finished according to the method of commentary.
263:
## 2. Cūḷavagga
## 1. Ratana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Yānīdha bhūtāni" is the Ratana Sutta. What is the reason for its origin (uppatti)? In the past, disasters such as famine arose in the city of Vesālī. To appease those dangers, the Licchavī princes went to Rājagaha, made a request, and brought the Blessed One to Vesālī. Having been brought thus, the Blessed One preached this sutta to calm those disasters. This is the summary here.

Ancient teachers, however, explain the origin of this Ratana Sutta in detail starting from the Story of Vesālī. That explanation should be understood thus: It is said that a fetus was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Knowing she was pregnant, she informed the King, and the King granted her pregnancy care (gabbhaparihāra). Having been well-protected, when the pregnancy matured, she entered the delivery chamber. Meritorious women usually give birth at the time of dawn, and she was one of them; therefore, at dawn, she gave birth to a lump of flesh (maṃsapesi) resembling a pot of lac or a Bandhujīvaka flower.

Then she thought, "Other queens give birth to sons resembling golden statues, but I, the Chief Queen, have given birth to a lump of flesh; disgrace will come upon me in the presence of the King." Fearing such disgrace, she placed that lump of flesh in a vessel, covered it, sealed it with the royal seal, and had it cast into the current of the Ganges. As soon as it was discarded by humans, deities arranged for its protection. They tied a gold plate to it, having written with cinnabar, "The offspring of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī." Then that vessel floated down the current of the Ganges, unhindered by dangers such as waves.

At that time, a certain ascetic lived on the bank of the Ganges, supported by a family of cowherds. Having gone down to the Ganges early in the morning, he saw the vessel coming and took it, thinking it was a refuse-heap cloth (paṃsukūla). Then, seeing the inscribed gold plate and the royal seal, he opened it and saw the lump of flesh. Upon seeing it, he thought, "This might be a fetus, for it has no foul or putrid smell." He took it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean spot. Then, after the lapse of half a month, it became two lumps of flesh. When the ascetic saw this, he kept them even more carefully. Then again, after the lapse of half a month, five buds appeared on each lump for the sake of hands, feet, and head. Then, after the lapse of half a month from that time...
264:
One lump of flesh became a boy resembling a golden statue, and the other became a girl. In the ascetic, a fatherly love for the children arose. Milk was produced from his thumb, and from then on, he obtained milk-rice. After eating the rice, he poured the milk into the mouths of the children. Whatever milk entered their stomachs was clearly visible from the outside, as if it were in a crystal vessel. In this way, they appeared to have no skin (nicchavi). Other teachers, however, say, "They had skin that was joined together as if it had been sewn." Thus, they became known as "Licchavī" either because of being skinless (nicchavitā) or because of having joined skin (līnacchavitā).

While raising the children, the ascetic would enter the village for alms late in the morning and return very late in the day. Knowing that his work was being hindered, the cowherds said, "Venerable sir, raising children is an obstacle for those who have gone forth. Give the children to us; we will raise them. May you perform only your own duties as a monk." The ascetic agreed, saying, "Very well." On the second day, the cowherds leveled the road, scattered flowers, raised banners and flags, and came to the hermitage playing musical instruments. The ascetic said, "These children are of great merit. Raise them with heedfulness so they may grow. When they are grown, perform the marriage ceremony between them. Please the King with the five bovine products (pañcagorasa), take a portion of land, and build a city. Consecrate the prince there." Having said this, he handed over the children. The cowherds agreed, saying, "Very well," and took the children away to raise them.

As the children grew up, while playing in places of dispute, they would strike other cowherd children with their hands and feet. Those children would cry. When asked by their parents, "Why are you crying?" they said, "These children, who have no parents and were raised by the ascetic, beat us severely." Then their parents said, "These children harass other children and cause them suffering. They should not be supported; they should be shunned (vajjitabba)." From then on, it is said that the region, measuring one hundred yojanas, was called "Vajjī." Then the cowherds pleased the King and obtained that region. They built a city right there, and having consecrated the sixteen-year-old prince, they made him King. They made a pact to marry him to that girl, saying, "No girl shall be brought from outside, and no girl from here shall be given to anyone else." From their first union, a son and a daughter (twins) were born. In this way, they were born in pairs sixteen times. Beyond that...
265:
When those children grew up in due order, the parks, houses, locations, and the wealth of their retinues could no longer be contained. Therefore, they surrounded the city with walls three times, each a gāvuta apart. Because the city was repeatedly enlarged (visālīkata), the name 'Vesālī' came into being. This is the story of the origin of the city of Vesālī.

This city of Vesālī was prosperous and extremely flourishing at the time the Blessed One appeared. In that city, there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings. Likewise, there were the same number of viceroys, generals, treasurers, and so forth. Regarding this, the Blessed One taught:

"At that time, Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food. There were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven palaces; seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven gabled houses; seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven parks; and seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven lotus ponds," as taught in the Mahāvagga.

At a later time, that city of Vesālī suffered from drought, crop failure, and famine. First, the poor people died, and their bodies were discarded outside the city. Due to the stench of the corpses, non-human beings (amanussa) entered the city. From then on, more people died, and because of the loathsomeness of those corpses, the ahivātaka disease (plague) broke out among living beings. Thus, oppressed by these three fears—famine, non-human beings, and disease—the citizens of Vesālī approached the King and said: "Great King, three kinds of fear have arisen in this city. Previously, up to seven generations of royal lineages, such fears never occurred. We think they have arisen now because of your unrighteousness." The King summoned everyone to the assembly hall and said, "Investigate my unrighteousness." They searched through all the traditional practices of the lineage but found no fault at all.

Then, finding no fault in the King, they pondered, "How can this fear be appeased for us?" Some among them suggested the six great teachers, saying, "The fear will be appeased just by their arrival." Others said, "It is heard that a Buddha has appeared in the world; that Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the benefit of all beings..."
266:
"The Blessed One possesses great psychic power and great majesty; all fears will be appeased just by His arrival." Because of those words, they were delighted and asked, "Where is that Blessed One residing now? Would He come if we sent an invitation?" Then others said, "Buddhas are compassionate; why would He not come? However, the Blessed One is currently residing in Rājagaha, and King Bimbisāra is attending to Him; perhaps that King might not allow Him to come." "In that case, let us persuade the King and then invite Him," they said. They sent two Licchavī princes with a large army and many gifts to the King, saying, "Persuade King Bimbisāra and bring the Blessed One." They went, presented the gifts to the King, reported the situation, and said, "Great King, please send the Blessed One to our city." The King did not directly consent but said, "You yourselves know what to do." 

Those princes approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, three fears have befallen our city. If the Blessed One were to come, it would be for our safety and welfare." The Blessed One, upon reflection, saw: "When the Ratana Sutta is recited in Vesālī, that protection will spread throughout a hundred thousand crores of world systems (cakkavāḷa), and at the conclusion of the Sutta, eighty-four thousand beings will attain Dhamma-realization." Thus, He accepted. Then King Bimbisāra, hearing of the Blessed One's acceptance, had it announced in the city by beat of drum: "The Blessed One has accepted the journey to Vesālī." He approached the Blessed One and asked, "Venerable Sir, is it true that You have accepted the journey to Vesālī?" "It is so, Great King," He replied. "In that case, Venerable Sir, please wait until I have prepared the road," the King requested.

Then King Bimbisāra leveled the ground for the five-yojana distance between Rājagaha and the Ganges River, built a monastery at every yojana, and then informed the Blessed One of the time for departure. The Blessed One set out, surrounded by five hundred monks. Along the five-yojana road, the King had flowers of five colors scattered knee-deep, erected banners, flags, full water pots, banana trees, and so on. He had two white umbrellas held over the Blessed One and one umbrella over each monk. Accompanied by his retinue, he made offerings of flowers and scents, had the Blessed One stay at each monastery, gave great offerings (mahādāna), and within five days, escorted Him to the banks of the Ganges. There, while decorating a boat with all kinds of ornaments, he sent a message to the people of Vesālī: "The Blessed One has arrived. Prepare the road and [receive] all of the Blessed One's..."
267: "Go and welcome [the Buddha]," [King Bimbisāra sent word]. Those Licchavī kings, thinking, "We will perform a worship twice as great as King Bimbisāra's," leveled the ground for three yojanas between Vesālī and the Ganges. They prepared four white umbrellas for the Blessed One and two white umbrellas for each monk, and while performing worship, they came and stood at the bank of the Ganges. King Bimbisāra joined two boats together, built a pavilion, decorated it with flower garlands and so on, and had a jeweled seat for the Buddha prepared on that raft. The Blessed One sat there. Five hundred monks also boarded the boat and sat in appropriate places. The King, following the Blessed One, waded into the water up to his neck and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall stay right here on the bank of the Ganges until the Blessed One returns," and then he turned back. Above, in the sky up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, the deities performed worship. Below, the Nagas living in the Ganges, such as Kambala and Assatara, performed worship. Thus, with great worship, the Blessed One traveled about one yojana on the Ganges and entered the boundary of the people of Vesālī. Then the Licchavī kings, performing worship twice as great as that done by King Bimbisāra, went out to welcome the Blessed One in water up to their necks. At that very moment, at that very instant, a great cloud arose from the four directions, thundering with vast masses of clouds of thick darkness spread with the light of lightning. Then, as soon as the Blessed One set His first footstep on the bank of the Ganges, the Pokkharavassa rain fell. Only those who wished to get wet got wet; those who did not wish to get wet did not get wet. In all places, water flowed to the depth of the knees, thighs, waist, and neck. All the carcasses were washed into the Ganges by the water, and the surface of the earth became extremely pure. The Licchavī kings had the Blessed One stay at every yojana along the way, giving great offerings, and performing double worship for three days, they led Him to the city of Vesālī. When the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, Sakka, the lord of the devas, arrived surrounded by a host of deities. Due to the assembly of powerful deities, the non-human beings (amanussa) mostly fled. The Blessed One, standing at the city gate, addressed the Elder Ānanda: "Ānanda, learn this Ratana Sutta, take the materials for offerings, and together with the Licchavī princes, wander between the three walls of Vesālī performing the protection (paritta)." Thus, He spoke the Ratana Sutta. In this way, the answers to the questions "By whom was this sutta spoken, when, where, and why?" have been described in detail by the ancient teachers starting from the Story of Vesālī.
268:
Thus, on the very day the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, having learned this Ratana Sutta which was spoken at the gate of Vesālī for the purpose of averting those calamities, the Venerable Ānanda, reciting it for the sake of protection, took water in the Blessed One's bowl and wandered through the entire city sprinkling it. As soon as the Elder said, "Yaṃ kiñci," those non-human beings who had not fled before and were staying near rubbish heaps, walls, and so on, fled through the four gates. The gates became so crowded that there was no space. Then, some non-human beings, unable to find an opening at the gates, fled by breaking through the city walls. As soon as the non-human beings left, the diseases in the bodies of the humans were appeased. Those people came out and worshipped the Elder with all kinds of perfumes, flowers, and so on. The multitude of people smeared the assembly hall (Santhāgāra) in the middle of the city with all kinds of perfumes, made a canopy, decorated it with all kinds of ornaments, and having prepared a suitable seat for the Buddha there, they invited the Blessed One.

The Blessed One entered the assembly hall and sat on the prepared seat. The community of monks, the kings, and the people also sat in appropriate places. Sakka, the lord of the devas, also sat nearby with the assembly of deities from the two deva worlds, as did other deities. The Elder Ānanda, having wandered through the whole of Vesālī and provided protection, came with the residents of Vesālī and sat on one side. There, the Blessed One spoke that same Ratana Sutta to everyone.

In that Ratana Sutta, in the first verse beginning with "yānīdha bhūtāni," the word "yāni" means whichever beings, whether of little power or great power. "Idha" means in this place, referring to the place of assembly at that moment. Regarding the word "bhūtāni," although the word "bhūta" occurs in the sense of "what is real" in such passages as "bhūtasmiṃ pācittiyaṃ"; in the sense of the five aggregates (khandha-pañcaka) in "bhūtamidanti, bhikkhave, samanupassatha"; in the sense of the four great elements (mahābhūta) such as the earth element in "cattāro kho, bhikkhu, mahābhūtā hetū"; in the sense of an Arahant (khīṇāsava) in "yo ca kālaghaso bhūto"; in the sense of all living beings in "sabbeva nikkhipissanti, bhūtā loke samussayaṃ"; in the sense of trees and so on in "bhūtagāmapātabyatāya"; and in the sense of the assembly of beings below the Cātumahārājikā devas in "bhūtaṃ bhūtato sañjānāti"—here, however, it should be understood generally as non-human beings (amanussa).
269:
"Samāgatāni" means those who have assembled together in harmony. "Bhummāni" means those born on the earth. The word "vā" is used in the sense of an alternative (vikappa). By that word "vā," having made one alternative as "whatever terrestrial deities are assembled here," He spoke "yāni vā antalikkhe" (or those in the sky) to make a second alternative. The meaning is: whatever deities born in the sky have assembled here. Herein, deities born from the Yāma realm up to the Akaniṭṭha realm should be understood as "deities in the sky" (antalikkhe bhūtāni) because they are born in celestial mansions (vimānas) appearing in the air. Below that, from Mount Sineru down to the ground, there are deities dwelling in trees, creepers, and so on. All those deities born on the earth and in things connected to the earth such as trees, creepers, and mountains should be understood as "terrestrial deities" (bhummāni bhūtāni).

Thus, the Blessed One, having distinguished all non-human beings (amanussa) with the two phrases "whether terrestrial or in the sky," then encompassed them with a single phrase, saying, "May all beings be happy-minded." "Sabbē" means all without exception. "Eva" is for emphasis, meaning not leaving out even one. "Bhūtā" refers to non-human beings (spirits/deities). "Sumanā bhavantu" means may they be happy-minded, reaching a state of joy and gladness. "Athopi" consists of two particles used at the beginning of a sentence to connect another matter. "Listen respectfully to what is spoken" (sakkacca suṇantu bhāsitaṃ) means: listen to my teaching, which brings celestial fortune and supramundane happiness, by being attentive, reflecting on it, and applying the whole mind.

In this way, in this verse, the Blessed One, having included the beings with the indefinite words "whatever beings are assembled here," then distinguished them into two types as "whether terrestrial or in the sky," then grouped them together as "all beings," and urged them toward the perfection of intention (āsayasampatti) with the words "may they be happy-minded." With the words "listen respectfully to what is spoken," He urged them toward the perfection of effort (payogasampatti), as well as the perfection of wise attention (yonisomanasikārasampatti) and the perfection of hearing from another (paratoghosasampatti). Likewise, He concluded the verse by urging them toward right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi), reliance on good persons (sappurisūpanissaya), and the perfection of the causes of concentration and wisdom.

"Tasmā hi bhūtā" is the second verse. Therein, "tasmā" is a word showing the reason. "Bhūtā" is a word of address (vocative). "Nisāmetha" means listen. "Sabbē" means...
270:
...all without exception. What is meant? Since you have abandoned your divine abodes and the abundance of enjoyments therein and have assembled here for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, and not for the purpose of seeing dances and such entertainment, therefore, O all spirits, listen (to my words).

Alternatively, seeing their happy state of mind and their desire to listen respectfully through the words "Sumanā bhavantu sakkaccaṃ suṇantu," He said: Since you are endowed with the purity of intention through happy-mindedness, right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi), and wise attention (yonisomanasikāra), and are endowed with the purity of effort (payogasuddi) through the basis of relying on good persons (sappurisūpanissaya) and hearing the Dhamma from another (paratoghosa) with a desire to listen respectfully, therefore, O all spirits, listen.

Alternatively, pointing out the reason for what was called "the spoken word" (bhāsitaṃ) at the end of the previous verse, He said: My spoken teaching is extremely rare. This is because the opportune moment (khana), which excludes the eight inopportune times (akkhana), is difficult to obtain. Because it proceeds from the virtues of wisdom and compassion, it also has many benefits. Desiring to speak that Dhamma, I said, "Listen to what is spoken." Therefore, O all spirits, listen—this is the meaning of this verse-line.

Thus, establishing that reason and urging them to listen to the teaching He spoke, He began to state the subject to be listened to: "Extend loving-kindness to the human race" (mettaṃ karotha mānusiyā pajāya).
