The meaning is: toward this human race afflicted by the three calamities, establish a state of friendship and a disposition for their welfare. Some teachers, however, read "mānusiyaṃ pajaṃ"; that is not suitable because the locative sense is not possible. The meaning explained by other teachers is also not suitable. The intention here is: I do not speak with the power of sovereignty, saying "I am the Buddha," but rather I speak for your benefit and for the benefit of this human race: "Extend loving-kindness to the human race."

"Whatever kings, having conquered the earth with its seven continents, and royal seers, while sacrificing, traveled around; the horse sacrifice (assamedha), the human sacrifice (purisamedha), the 'peg-throwing' sacrifice (sammāpāsa), the 'drink of victory' (vājapeyya), and the 'unbarred' sacrifice (niraggaḷa); these sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the well-developed heart of loving-kindness."
271:
“If a person with a mind free from malice develops loving-kindness even towards a single being, he becomes virtuous through that. And being compassionate in mind towards all beings, the noble one who performs much merit is great.” (A. Ni. 8.1) — Through the power of such suttas and through the power of the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, it should be understood that loving-kindness is beneficial to those who practice it.

“A person who is pitied by the devas always sees auspicious things.” (Dī. Ni. 2.153, Udā. 76, Mahāva. 286) — Through the power of such suttas, it should be understood that loving-kindness is also beneficial to those towards whom it is directed.

Desiring to show the beneficial nature for both parties in this way, after saying, “Show loving-kindness to the human race,” the Buddha now said, “They bring offerings day and night, therefore protect them diligently,” to show their helpfulness. The meaning of that verse is: O devas, those humans who make deva-images out of paintings, woodcarvings, etc., and approach shrines, trees, etc., to make offerings (bali) during the day dedicated to the devas, and also make offerings at night during the waning moon and so on. Or, by giving food distributed by tickets (salāka-bhatta) and so on, they make offerings during the day by sharing the merit (patti-dāna) with devas ranging from guardian devas up to the Brahma devas. By having umbrellas raised, lamps lit, and all-night Dhamma recitations performed, they also make offerings at night by sharing the merit. Why should such people not be protected? Since they thus make offerings dedicated to you day and night without fail, therefore protect those people. For the reason of making such offerings, you devas should protect and guard those humans, remove what is harmful to them, and bring what is beneficial. Being diligent and keeping that sense of gratitude in your hearts, protect them by constantly remembering them.

Having thus shown the helpfulness of humans towards devas, the Buddha began to utter the words of truth (sacca-vacana) starting with “Yaṃ kiñci vittaṃ” (Whatever wealth...) in order to appease the dangers of those humans and to enable devas and humans to hear the Dhamma by proclaiming the virtues of the Buddha and so on. In that phrase, “Yaṃ kiñci” includes everything without exception and without limitation, in various places...
272:
...it refers to wealth suitable for trade. “Vittaṃ” means wealth. It is called “vitta” because it generates delight (vitti). By the phrase “idha vā,” the human world is indicated; by “huraṃ vā,” the other remaining worlds are indicated. Although the phrase “huraṃ vā” could include the entire world excluding humans, because “saggesu vā” is mentioned later, it should be understood as taking the remaining beings like Nāgas and Supaṇṇas (Garudas), excluding both humans and devas. Thus, by these two phrases, the wealth of humans suitable for trade and for use as ornaments—such as gold, silver, pearls, gems, cat’s-eye, coral, rubies, and variegated gems—is indicated, as well as the wealth of Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, etc., which arises in jewel-filled mansions (vimānas) spanning hundreds of yojanas with grounds covered in pearl and gem sands.

“Saggesu vā” refers to the Sense-sphere (Kāmāvacara) and Fine-material-sphere (Rūpāvacara) deva worlds. They are called “sagga” because they are attained or reached through beautiful kamma, or because they are supremely excellent. “Yaṃ” refers to wealth, whether owned or unowned. “Ratanaṃ” (Jewel) is so called because it brings, carries, generates, or increases delight (rati). Anything that is esteemed, high-priced, incomparable, rare to see, and used by noble beings is called a jewel. Accordingly, it was said:

“Because it is esteemed, high-priced, incomparable, rare to see, and used by noble beings, it is called a jewel.”

“Paṇītaṃ” means excellent, superior, or that which is hard to be satiated with. Thus, by this verse-phrase, the owned jewels in the all-jeweled mansions like Sudhammā and Vejayanta in the heavens, which span hundreds of yojanas, are indicated; as well as the unowned jewels associated with empty mansions when beings are mostly reborn in woeful states due to the absence of a Buddha’s appearance; and also other unowned jewels depending on the earth, the great ocean, the Himalayas, and so on.

In the phrase “Na no samaṃ atthi Tathāgatena,” “na” is used for negation and “no” for emphasis. “Samaṃ” means equal, “atthi” means exists, and “Tathāgatena” means with the Buddha. What is meant? Among all the wealth and jewels described, there is not even a single jewel equal to the Buddha-jewel. Indeed, there are the Wheel-jewel and the Gem-jewel of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), which are called jewels in the sense of being esteemed. When they appear, the great multitude does not esteem other things. No one takes flowers, scents, etc., to go to the places of Yakkhas or spirits; instead, all people esteem and honor only the Wheel-jewel and the Gem-jewel. They pray for great boons from them, and for some, those prayed-for boons are fulfilled.
273:
That jewel, too, is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. If a jewel is so called because of the sense of being cherished and esteemed, then only the Tathāgata is truly a jewel. For when the Tathāgata appears, deities and humans of great power do not show such esteem to anyone else, nor do they worship anyone else. Thus, Brahmā Sahampati worshipped the Tathāgata with a garland of jewels as large as Mount Sineru; other deities and humans, such as King Bimbisāra, King Kosala, and Anāthapiṇḍika, also worshipped him according to their ability. Even after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the great King Asoka, dedicating himself to the Buddha, spent ninety-six crores of wealth and established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the whole of Jambudīpa; what need is there to mention the esteem shown by others? Furthermore, for whom else who has attained Parinibbāna is such esteem and reverence shown—towards the places of his birth, enlightenment, turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and Parinibbāna, or towards his images and stupas—as is shown to the Blessed One? Thus, in the sense of being cherished and esteemed, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Likewise, there is a jewel in the sense of being of great value, namely, Kāsika cloth. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, Kāsika cloth, even when worn out, is beautiful in color, pleasant to the touch, and of great value." Yet even that Kāsika cloth is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. If a jewel is so called because of being of great value, then only the Tathāgata is truly a jewel. For the Tathāgata, even when he accepts a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) from people, it brings them great fruit and great benefit, just as it did for King Asoka. This is his quality of being of great value. To show that there is no fault in saying he is of great value, this scriptural passage should be understood as evidence:

"Monks, for those from whom the Blessed One accepts the four requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift brings them great fruit and great benefit. This, I say, is the quality of the Blessed One being of great value. Monks, just as Kāsika cloth is of great value, so too, monks, do I speak of this person."

Thus, in the sense of being of great value, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Likewise, there is a jewel in the sense of being incomparable. This is the Wheel-jewel (Cakka-ratana) of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), which arises with a hub made of sapphire (indanīla), a thousand spokes made of the seven jewels, a rim made of coral, and joints made of red gold. Above every ten spokes of that Wheel-jewel, there is a single ornament (muṇḍāra)...
274:
...for the purpose of making a sound by catching the wind. The sound produced by that wind is like the sound of a well-played five-fold musical ensemble (pañcaṅgika-tūriya). On both sides of the hub of that Wheel-jewel, there are two lion faces. Inside, it is hollow like a cartwheel. There is no maker or creator of that Wheel-jewel; it arises due to weather (utu) conditioned by kamma. When the King has fulfilled the ten-fold duties of a Universal Monarch, and on the full-moon Uposatha day, having washed his head and observing the Uposatha precepts, while he sits reflecting on his virtue in the noble palace, he sees it rising like the full moon or the sun. The sound of that Wheel-jewel is heard from twelve yojanas away, and its color is seen from one yojana away. While the people look on with great wonder, thinking, "A second moon or sun has surely arisen," it comes over the city and remains at the eastern side of the King's inner palace, neither too high nor too low, as if fixed by an axle, at a place suitable for the people to worship with scents and flowers.

Following that Wheel-jewel, the Elephant-jewel (Hatthi-ratana) appears. That elephant is entirely white with red feet, stands firmly on seven points, possesses psychic power, and can travel through the air. It comes from either the Uposatha elephant lineage or the Chaddanta elephant lineage. If it comes from the Uposatha lineage, the eldest elephant comes; if from the Chaddanta lineage, the youngest elephant comes. That elephant is well-trained in arts and endowed with gentleness. Carrying a retinue of twelve yojanas, that Elephant-jewel can travel around the entire continent and return to its royal capital even before breakfast.

Following that Elephant-jewel, the Horse-jewel (Assa-ratana) appears. It is entirely white with red feet, has a head like a crow's, and a mane like muñja grass. It comes from the Valāhaka king of horses lineage. The remaining details are the same as those of the Elephant-jewel.

Following that Horse-jewel, the Gem-jewel (Maṇi-ratana) appears. That Gem-jewel is a beryl (veḷuriya), beautiful, of authentic quality, eight-faceted, and well-polished. In length, it is like the hub of the Wheel. It comes from Mount Vepulla. Even in four-fold darkness, that Gem-jewel, placed at the top of the King's banner, illuminates for a distance of one yojana. By that light, people think, "It is daytime," and engage in their work; they can see even the smallest ants.
275:
Following that Gem-treasure, the Woman-treasure appears. She is either the King's regular chief queen, or she comes from Uttarakuru, or from the royal family of Madda. She is free from the six defects such as being too tall and so forth; she possesses an appearance that surpasses human beauty but has not yet reached divine beauty. The limbs of that Woman-treasure are warm when it is cold and cool when it is hot. Her touch is like a tuft of cotton-wool that has been beaten a hundred times. The fragrance of sandalwood wafts from her body, and the fragrance of blue lotus wafts from her mouth. She is endowed with various special qualities, such as being the first to rise.

Following that Woman-treasure, the Householder-treasure appears. The householder who is the King's regular treasurer is the Householder-treasure. As soon as the Wheel-treasure appears to that Householder-treasure, the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) arises. With that divine eye, he can see hidden treasures, whether they have an owner or are ownerless, within a distance of one league (yojana) all around. That Householder-treasure approaches the King and invites him, saying: "Your Majesty, may you be free from worry; I shall perform the duties required of wealth with your wealth."

Following that Householder-treasure, the Counselor-treasure (pariṇāyaka-ratana) appears. The King's regular eldest son is the Counselor-treasure. As soon as the Wheel-treasure appears, he becomes endowed with extraordinary wisdom and proficiency. He is capable of knowing the minds of the assembly within twelve leagues with his own mind, and is able to restrain or encourage them. That Counselor approaches the King and invites him, saying: "Your Majesty, may you be free from worry; I shall administer the kingdom for you." Any other such thing is called a treasure in the sense of being incomparable. It is not possible to value such a treasure by comparing or weighing it, saying: "It is worth a hundred, or a thousand, or ten million." Among all those treasures, there is no treasure equal to the Buddha-treasure. If something is called a treasure in the sense of being incomparable, then only the Tathāgata is truly a treasure. No one is able to define the Tathāgata by comparing or weighing him against anyone else in terms of virtue, concentration, wisdom, or any other quality, saying: "He has this much quality, or he is equal to this person, or he is similar to this person." Thus, in the sense of being incomparable, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, something is called a treasure in the sense of being rare to behold. How so? The Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) and his treasures, such as the Wheel-treasure, which appear very rarely, are called treasures in the sense of being rare to behold. Even those treasures are not equal to the Buddha-treasure. If something is called a treasure in the sense of being rare to behold, then only the Tathāgata is truly a treasure. How can there be the state of being a treasure for Universal Monarchs and others who appear in great numbers even within a single aeon? Because for many incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) aeons, the world is void of a Tathāgata...
276:
...the world is void (of a Buddha for incalculable aeons); therefore, the Tathāgata is rare to behold because he appears only once in a long while. This was spoken by the Blessed One at the time of his Parinibbāna: "Ānanda, the deities are complaining: 'We have come from afar to see the Tathāgata. Tathāgatas, the Worthy Ones, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, appear in the world only once in a long while. In the last watch of this very night, the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna will take place. And this influential monk stands in front of the Blessed One, blocking him; we do not get the opportunity to see the Tathāgata in his final hour.'"

Thus, in the sense of being rare to behold, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, something is called a treasure in the sense of being used by noble beings (anoma-satta-paribhoga). These are the Wheel-treasure and so forth of the Universal Monarch. That Wheel-treasure does not appear for the use of those of low birth and inferior men, such as the Caṇḍāla, Veṇa, Nesāda, Rathakāra, and Pukkusa, even in their dreams, even if they possess a hundred billion in wealth or live in a noble seven-storied palace. Because it appears for the use only of a King of the warrior caste (Khattiya) who is well-born on both sides and who has fulfilled the tenfold duties of a Universal Monarch, it is indeed an object for the use of noble beings. Even that Wheel-treasure is not equal to the Buddha-treasure. If something is called a treasure in the sense of being used by noble beings, then only the Tathāgata is truly a treasure.

This is because the Tathāgata is not for the use (seeing or attending upon) even in dreams of the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others of similar nature, who, although regarded as noble beings in the world, are not endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya) and have wrong views. He is for the use (seeing or attending upon) only of the Great Disciples born of noble families and others such as Bāhiya Dāruciriya, who are endowed with the supporting conditions and possess the penetrative knowledge and vision capable of attaining Arahantship even at the end of a single verse. They use (attend upon) him in various ways, accomplishing the supreme seeing (dassanānuttariya), the supreme hearing (savanānuttariya), the supreme service (pāricariyānuttariya), and so forth. Thus, in the sense of being used by noble beings, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata.

In the sense of producing delight (rati-janana) without distinction, something is also called a treasure. This is the Wheel-treasure of the Universal Monarch. Upon seeing that Wheel-treasure, the Universal Monarch becomes joyful; thus, that treasure produces delight for the King. Furthermore, the Universal Monarch, holding a golden pitcher in his left hand, sprinkles (consecrates) the Wheel-treasure with his right hand...
277:
“May the noble Wheel Treasure turn! May the noble Wheel Treasure conquer!” (Saying this, he performs the consecration). Then, the Wheel Treasure, emitting a melodious sound like that of the five-fold musical instruments, travels through the sky towards the eastern direction. By the power of the Wheel Treasure, the Universal Monarch also follows with his four-fold army, twelve yojanas in width, traveling neither too high nor too low—passing beneath tall trees and above short trees. He accepts gifts from the hands of those who come bearing offerings such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts from the trees. He proceeds while admonishing the rival kings who come with great humility, saying, “Come, Great King,” and instructing them with principles such as, “Living beings must not be killed.”

Wherever the Universal Monarch wishes to eat or to take a midday rest, there the Wheel Treasure descends from the sky and remains stationary, as if its axle were firmly fixed, on a level piece of ground suitable for all purposes such as water supply. When the desire to travel arises again in the King, it proceeds as before, making its sound. Hearing that sound, the retinue, also twelve yojanas in extent, follows through the sky. The Wheel Treasure gradually descends into the eastern ocean. As it descends, the water recedes about one yojana and stands like a wall. The multitude of people gathers the seven kinds of treasures as they please. Then the King, holding a golden pitcher, pours the water of consecration, saying, “From this point forward, let this be my kingdom,” and turns back. The army leads the way, the Wheel Treasure follows behind, and the King remains in the middle. The water refills the places from which the Wheel Treasure has withdrawn. In this same manner, it travels to the southern, western, and northern oceans.

After thus traversing the four directions, the Wheel Treasure ascends into the sky to a height of three yojanas. Standing there in the sky, the King, by the power of the Wheel Treasure, surveys the entire universe as if it were a forest of blooming lotuses—including Pubbavideha island, which is seven thousand yojanas in circumference and surrounded by five hundred small islands; Uttarakuru island, which is eight thousand yojanas in circumference; Aparagoyāna island, which is also seven thousand yojanas in circumference; and Jambudīpa island, which is ten thousand yojanas in circumference—thus the four great continents adorned with two thousand small islands. As he surveys them, an immeasurable delight arises in the King. In this way, that Wheel Treasure generates delight for the King; yet, even that is not equal to the Buddha-treasure. If something is called a ‘treasure’ because it generates delight, then only the Tathāgata is truly a treasure. What can this Wheel Treasure do? For the delight of a Universal Monarch generated by all treasures such as the Wheel Treasure does not reach even a fraction, a part, or a portion of the divine delight with which the Tathāgata (is endowed)...
278:
...does not reach [the delight of the Buddha]; moreover, the Tathāgata generates a delight that is far superior and more sublime than the delight of the Universal Monarch's treasures. He generates the delight of the first jhāna, the delight of the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas, the delight of the sphere of infinite space, the delight of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the delight of the path of stream-entry, the delight of the fruit of stream-entry, and the delight of the paths and fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship for countless devas and humans who follow his instructions. Thus, because he generates such delight, there is no treasure equal to the Buddha.

Furthermore, what is called a ‘treasure’ is of two kinds: animate (saviññāṇaka) and inanimate (aviññāṇaka). Among these, inanimate treasures are the Wheel Treasure, the Gem Treasure, or any other thing not connected with the senses, such as gold and silver. Animate treasures are those from the Elephant Treasure down to the Counselor Treasure, or any other such thing connected with the senses. Between these two kinds, the animate treasure is declared supreme. Why? Because inanimate treasures like gold, silver, gems, and pearls are brought for the purpose of adorning animate treasures like the Elephant Treasure.

Animate treasures are also of two kinds: animal treasures and human treasures. Among these, the human treasure is declared supreme. Why? Because the animal treasure serves as a mount for the human treasure. Human treasures are also of two kinds: the female treasure and the male treasure. Among these, the male treasure is declared supreme. Why? Because the female treasure becomes an attendant to the male treasure. Male treasures are also of two kinds: the householder (agārika) treasure and the homeless (anagārika) treasure. Among these, the homeless treasure is declared supreme. Why? Because even the Universal Monarch, who is the supreme among householder treasures, bows with the five-fold prostration to a homeless treasure endowed with virtues such as morality, and by serving and associating with him, attains the prosperity of devas and humans, and finally reaches the bliss of Nibbāna.

In this way, the homeless treasure is also of two kinds: the Noble One (ariya) and the worldling (puthujjana). The Noble treasure is of two kinds: the trainee (sekha) and the non-trainee (asekha). The non-trainee treasure is of two kinds: the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and the serenity-vehicle practitioner (samathayānika). The serenity-vehicle treasure is of two kinds: those who have reached the perfection of a disciple (sāvaka-pāramī) and those who have not. Among these, the one who has reached the perfection of a disciple is declared supreme because of the greatness of their qualities. Superior even to the treasure of one who has reached the perfection of a disciple is the Paccekabuddha treasure, declared supreme because of the greatness of their qualities. Indeed, even hundreds of disciples equal to Sāriputta and Moggallāna do not reach even a hundredth part of the qualities of a single Paccekabuddha. Superior even to the Paccekabuddha treasure is the Sammāsambuddha treasure, declared the most supreme because of the extraordinary greatness of his qualities. In fact, even if the entire Jambudīpa were filled with Paccekabuddhas sitting cross-legged with their knees touching, they would not reach the number, the part, or (the portion of the qualities of a single Sammāsambuddha).
279:
Even Paccekabuddhas cannot reach even a hundredth part of the Buddha's qualities. It is true that the Blessed One said: "Monks, among whatever beings there are, whether footless... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them" and so forth. Thus, in no way is there any jewel equal to the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "There is no jewel equal to us, equal to the Tathāgata."

Having thus spoken of the Buddha-jewel's incomparability with other jewels, now, in order to appease the dangers that had arisen for those beings, without relying on birth, lineage, status as a clansman, or beauty of complexion, but rather relying on the Buddha-jewel's peerless nature due to qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi) in the world from the Avīci hell up to the highest plane of existence (bhavagga), he uttered this word of truth: "This too is a precious jewel in the Buddha; by this truth, may there be well-being."

The meaning of that verse is: Whatever pleasing treasure or jewel exists in this world, or in the world of Nagas and Garudas, or in the heavens and Brahma realms, the Buddha-jewel is sublime, being unequal to those treasures due to various qualities. If this statement is true, by this word of truth, may there be well-being for these living beings; may there be the existence of those who desire good, freedom from disease, and freedom from danger. Here, just as in "Ānanda, the eye is empty of self or what belongs to self," it should be understood as "by way of being a self" or "by way of what belongs to a self." Otherwise, it would mean that the eye is not prohibited from being a self or belonging to a self. Similarly, "ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ" means the state of being a jewel is sublime, the nature of being a jewel is sublime. Otherwise, it would result in the Buddha himself not being the jewel. For a thing that possesses a jewel is not necessarily called a jewel. However, because there is the state of being a jewel (ratanatta) consisting of meanings such as being honored, which is connected in various ways, it is designated as a "jewel" based on that state of being a jewel; thus it is established as a jewel because of the existence of that "jewel-ness." Alternatively, by the reason "This too is a precious jewel in the Buddha," it should be understood that the Buddha himself is the jewel. As soon as the Blessed One recited this verse, well-being arose for the royal family and the dangers were appeased. The authority of this verse was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred billion world-systems.

Having thus spoken the truth by the qualities of the Buddha, he now began to speak by the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna with "Khayaṃ virāgaṃ..." In that regard, because through the realization of Nibbāna, lust and so forth are exhausted, completely exhausted; or because it is merely the exhaustion of their non-arising and cessation; or because...
280:
And because it is free from lust and so forth, both in terms of association and object; or because when that Nibbāna is realized, lust and so forth are absolutely faded away, gone, and destroyed; therefore it is called "Khaya" (Exhaustion) and "Virāga" (Detachment). Furthermore, because its arising is not perceived, nor its passing away, nor the alteration of what stays, it does not take birth, does not age, and does not die; thus it is called "Amata" (the Deathless). It is called "Paṇīta" (Sublime) in the sense of being excellent and in the sense of not being distressing.

"Yadajjhagā" means that Nibbāna which he attained, found, and realized through the power of his own knowledge. "Sakyamuni" means he is "Sakya" because he was born into the Sakyan clan, and "Muni" because he is endowed with the state of a sage (moneyya-dhamma); being a sage of the Sakyan clan, he is "Sakyamuni." "Samāhita" means one whose mind is concentrated through the concentration of the Noble Path. "Na tena dhammena samatthi kiñci" means there is no state of Dhamma equal to that Dhamma known as "Exhaustion" and so forth, attained by the Sakyan Sage. Therefore, it is also said in another Sutta: "Monks, among whatever things there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, detachment (virāga) is declared the foremost of them" and so forth.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the Dhamma of Nibbāna's incomparability with other dhammas, now, in order to appease the dangers that had arisen for those beings, relying on the peerless nature of the Dhamma-jewel of Nibbāna through the qualities of exhaustion, detachment, the deathless, and the sublime, he uttered the word of truth: "This too is a precious jewel in the Dhamma; by this truth, may there be well-being." The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same way as explained in the previous verse. The authority of this verse was also accepted by non-human beings in a hundred billion world-systems.

Having thus spoken the truth by the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna, he now intended to speak by the qualities of the Dhamma of the Path, and thus uttered the verse beginning with "Yaṃ buddhasettho." In that verse, he is "Buddha" because he "realized the truths" and so forth; he is "Settha" because he is excellent and praiseworthy; being both Buddha and excellent, he is "Buddhasettha." Or, he is "Buddhasettha" because he is the most excellent among the Buddhas known as Anubuddhas and Paccekabuddhas. That Excellent Buddha praised and revealed that Path in various places in such ways as: "And of paths, the eightfold is the best, the secure way to the attainment of Nibbāna," and "Monks, I will teach you the noble right concentration with its causes and requisites." "Suciṃ" (Pure) means it is an extremely pure Dhamma because it brings about the total uprooting of the stains of defilements. "Samādhimānantarikaññamāhu" refers to that concentration of the Path which is called "Anantarika-samādhi" (Immediate Concentration) because it gives its fruit immediately after its own occurrence without fail. Indeed, when the concentration of the Path has arisen, there is no obstacle that can prevent the arising of its fruit. As it is said:
281: "This person is also practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry; if it were the time for the world to burn, the world would not burn as long as this person has not realized the fruit of Stream-entry. This person is called a 'ṭhitakappī'—one who stays for an aeon. All those who are endowed with the Path are also called ṭhitakappī," thus it is said (in the Puggala-paññatti). "Samādhinā tena samo na vijjati" means that there is no concentration of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere equal to that pure Ānantarika-samādhi (the concentration of the Path of Arahantship) which the Excellent Buddha especially praised. Why? Because even if one is born in various Brahma worlds by developing those fine-material and immaterial concentrations, there is still the possibility of being reborn in hell and other woeful states. However, for the Noble One who has developed this concentration of the Path of Arahantship, it is possible to completely eradicate all future rebirths. Therefore, it was also said in another Sutta: "Monks, as far as there are conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is said to be the foremost among them," and so on. In this way, the Blessed One, having stated that the Ānantarika-samādhi is incomparable to other concentrations, now performs an act of truth based on the peerless nature of the jewel of the Path, just as in the previous method: "This jewel in the Path is also excellent; by this truth, may there be well-being!" The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. The authority of this verse was also accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand million world systems. Having thus spoken the truth through the virtues of the Path, he now begins to speak through the virtues of the Saṅgha: "Ye puggalā" (Those persons). In that verse, "ye" is an indefinite pronoun. "Puggalā" means beings. "Aṭṭha" (eight) is the term defining their number. Indeed, they are eight because there are four practicing the Path and four established in the Fruit. "Sataṃ pasatthā" means they are praised by the virtuous—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other devas and humans. Why? Because they are endowed with innate virtues such as virtue (sīla). For those Noble Ones, there are innate virtues like virtue and concentration, just as there are innate colors and scents in flowers like the campaka, vakula, and jasmine. Therefore, like flowers endowed with color and scent, they are always dear, pleasing, and worthy of praise to devas and humans. Thus it is said: "Ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā." Alternatively, "ye" is an indefinite pronoun. "Puggalā" means beings. "Aṭṭhasataṃ" (one hundred and eight) is the term defining their number. Indeed, those persons are the Ekabījī, the Kolaṃkola...
282: ...the three types of Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) starting with the Sattakkhattuparama; the three types of Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī) who have attained the fruit in the sense sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere—all these (six) persons become twenty-four through the four modes of progress (paṭipadā). There are five (Non-returners) in the Aviha realm: the Antarā-parinibbāyī, Upahacca-parinibbāyī, Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī, Asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī, and Uddhaṃsoto-akaniṭṭhagāmī. Likewise, there are five in each of the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, there are four, excluding the Uddhaṃsoto. Thus, there are twenty-four Non-returners (Anāgāmī). There are two types of Arahants: the Sukkhavipassaka Arahant and the Samathayānika Arahant. With the four persons on the Path (Maggaṭṭha), the total is fifty-four. All these (fifty-four) persons, when doubled by the power of the faith-led (saddhā-dhura) and wisdom-led (paññā-dhura) faculties, become one hundred and eight. The remaining explanation is the same as previously mentioned. "Cattāရိ etāni yugāni honti" (These are four pairs) means that although all those persons are eight or one hundred and eight in detail, in brief, the one on the Path of Stream-entry and the one in the Fruit of Stream-entry make one pair; thus, up to the one on the Path of Arahantship and the one in the Fruit of Arahantship, there are four pairs. In the phrase "te dakkhiṇeyyā," the word "te" (they) specifically identifies the persons previously mentioned indefinitely. Those persons who are eight or one hundred and eight in detail, or four pairs in brief, are called "dakkhiṇeyyā" because they are worthy of noble offerings (dakkhiṇā). "Dakkhiṇā" refers to a gift given with faith in kamma and its result, without expecting services such as medical treatment or running errands. Persons endowed with virtues like virtue (sīla) are worthy of such offerings. Since these persons are also endowed with such virtues, they are called "dakkhiṇeyyā." "Sugatassa sāvakā" (Disciples of the Sugata) means the Blessed One is called "Sugata" because he is endowed with an excellent manner of going, because he has gone to the beautiful state (Nibbāna), because he has gone well, and because he has spoken well. Those who listen to the teachings of that Sugata are called "sāvakā" (disciples). Although others also listen to the teachings, they do not perform the duties to be done after listening. These persons, however, having listened, practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti) and reach the paths and fruits; therefore, they are called "sāvakā." "Etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni" means that even small gifts given to these disciples of the Sugata yield great fruit because of the purity of the recipient. Therefore, it was also said in the Sutta: "Monks, as far as there are communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's disciples is said to be the foremost among them, namely, the four pairs of men, the eight individuals; this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples... the result is great."
283:
In this way, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of all those established in the Paths and Fruits, now utters the statement of truth beginning with "Idam-pi saṅghe" (This too in the Saṅgha), based on those very virtues. The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The authority of this verse is accepted by the non-human beings (deities) in the hundred thousand crores of world-systems.

Having thus spoken the truth based on the virtues of the Saṅgha by way of those established in the Paths and Fruits, he now begins to speak of the virtues of certain Arahants who are experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition, with the verse beginning "Ye suppayuttā" (Those well-applied). In that verse, the word "Ye" (Those) is an indefinite demonstrative. "Suppayuttā" means well-applied; it refers to those who, having abandoned various forms of wrong livelihood (anesana) and relying on a pure livelihood, have begun to apply themselves well to insight (vipassanā). Alternatively, "suppayuttā" means those endowed with pure bodily and verbal actions. By this term, he shows their aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). "Manasā daḷhena" means with a firm mind, with a mind endowed with stable concentration (samādhi). By this term, he shows their aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). "Nikkāmino" means those who, without regard for body or life, have made their departure from all defilements through energy (vīriya) led by wisdom (paññā). By this term, he shows their aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) endowed with energy.

"Gotama-sāsanamhi" means in the Dispensation of the Tathāgata, who is Gotama by clan. By this term, he points out the absence of departure from defilements for those outside this Dispensation who perform various "immortal penances" (amaratappa), due to the absence of virtues such as right application. The word "Te" (They) refers back to the persons previously mentioned. In the term "pattipattā", "patti" means that which is to be attained; "patti" is a name for the Fruit of Arahantship, which is worthy of being attained and upon reaching which one becomes supremely secure from bondage (yogakkhema). Those who have reached such an attainment are "pattipattā". "Amata" is Nibbāna. "Vigayha" means having entered into it by way of the object. "Laddhā" means having obtained. "Mudhā" means freely, without paying any price (not even a farthing/kākaṇika). "Nibbuti" means the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) in which the distress of defilements is stilled. "Bhuñjamānā" means experiencing.

What is meant is this: Those who, in this Dispensation of Gotama, are well-applied (suppayuttā) because they are perfect in virtue, possess firm minds (manasā daḷhena) because they are perfect in concentration, and are free from defilements (nikkāmino) because they are perfect in wisdom—they, having entered into Nibbāna through this right practice and experiencing the peace called the attainment of fruition obtained freely, are called those who have reached the attainment (pattipattā).

In this way, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of the Arahants who experience the bliss of the attainment of fruition, now based on those very virtues, [utters] the statement of truth...
284:
...utters the statement of truth beginning with "Idam-pi saṅghe". The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The authority of this verse is also accepted by the non-human beings (deities) in the hundred thousand crores of world-systems.

Having thus spoken the truth based on the Saṅgha through the virtues of the Arahants, he now begins to speak of the virtues of the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), who is evident to the many, with the verse beginning "Yathindakhīlo". In that verse, "Yathā" is a word of comparison (simile). "Indakhīlo" is the name of a pillar made of heartwood, which is struck into the ground after digging eight or ten cubits deep inside the threshold for the purpose of securing the city gate. "Pathaviṃ" means into the earth. "Sito" means having entered within and being supported (firmly fixed). "Siyā" means it would be. "Catubbhi vātehi" means by winds coming from the four directions. "Asampakampiyo" means unable to be shaken or moved. "Tathūpamaṃ" means having such a simile. "Sappurisaṃ" means the superior man. "Vadāmi" means I, the Buddha, say. "Yo ariyasaccāni avecca passati" means that Stream-enterer who sees the four Noble Truths, having penetrated them with wisdom. In that statement, the Noble Truths should be understood in the manner stated in the Visuddhimagga.

The summary of the meaning here is: Just as a city pillar (indakhīla), because of its deep foundation, is fixed in the earth and cannot be shaken by winds from the four directions, so too I, the Buddha, declare this virtuous man, who sees the Noble Truths with penetration, to be like that pillar. Why? Because just as that city pillar is unshakeable by the four winds, so too is he unshakeable by the winds of the doctrines of all sectarians (titthiya). Because of that vision, no one is able to shake or move him. Therefore, it is also said in another Sutta:

"Monks, just as an iron pillar or a city pillar (indakhīla) with a deep foundation, well-planted, is motionless and unshakeable; even if a fierce storm of wind and rain should come from the eastern direction, it could not shake it, could not make it tremble, could not move it. Even if it should come from the western... southern... northern direction, it could not move it. For what reason? Because of the depth of the foundation, monks, and because the city pillar is well-planted. Even so, monks, whatever recluses or brahmins understand as it really is: 'This is suffering... this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,' they [do not look to] another..."
285: They do not look at the face of an ascetic or a brahmin, thinking, 'This venerable one, knowing, truly knows; seeing, truly sees.' Why is that? Monks, it is because the Four Noble Truths have been well seen (SN 5.1109). Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Jewel of the Sangha by way of the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) who is evident to the multitude, now employs the word of truth based on those very virtues: 'Idampi saṅghe...' (This too in the Sangha). The meaning of this should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The authority of this verse is accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand crores of world systems. Having thus spoken the truth based on the Sangha through the virtues of a Stream-enterer without distinction, he now begins to speak by way of the three types of Stream-enterers: the One-seeder (Ekabījī), the Family-to-family (Kolaṅkola), and the Seven-times-at-most (Sattakkhattuparama). The Blessed One said: 'Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, becomes a Stream-enterer... Having been reborn only once more, he makes an end of suffering; this one is called a One-seeder (Ekabījī). Likewise, having wandered and roamed through two or three families, he makes an end of suffering; this one is called a Family-to-family (Kolaṅkola). Likewise, having wandered and roamed among devas and humans for seven times at most, he makes an end of suffering; this one is called a Seven-times-at-most (Sattakkhattuparama)' (Pp. 31-33). He began to speak the verse 'Ye ariyasaccāni' (Those who [clearly see] the Noble Truths) by way of the virtue of the Sattakkhattuparama, who is the youngest among those three types of Stream-enterers. In that verse, 'Ye ariyasaccāni' is as previously explained. 'Vibhāvayanti' means they destroy the darkness of defilements that shroud the truths with the light of wisdom, making the truths manifest and clear to themselves. 'Gambhīrapaññena' (By him of deep wisdom) refers to the Omniscient Buddha, who possesses wisdom that cannot be fathomed by the knowledge of the world including the devas, due to his immeasurable wisdom. 'Sudesitāni' means well-taught through various methods such as brevity, detail, completeness, and so on. 'Kiñcāpi te honti bhusaṃ pamattā' (Even if they are greatly negligent) means that although those persons who have clearly seen the Noble Truths may be greatly negligent due to grounds for negligence such as divine kingship or the status of a Wheel-turning Monarch, nevertheless, because of the cessation of kammic-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) through the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, except for...
286: ...the mind-and-matter (nāma-rūpa) that would have arisen in the beginningless saṃsāra, because of their cessation and disappearance, they do not take an eighth birth; rather, having undertaken insight (vipassanā) in the seventh birth itself, they attain Arahatship. Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Jewel of the Sangha by way of the Sattakkhattuparama, now employs the word of truth based on those very virtues: 'Idampi saṅghe...' The meaning of this should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The authority of this verse is accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand crores of world systems. Having thus spoken the truth based on the Sangha through the virtue of the Sattakkhattuparama not taking an eighth birth, he now begins to speak the verse 'Sahāvassa' to describe the distinguished virtue of that same Sattakkhattuparama, who, though taking seven births, is superior to other persons who have not abandoned the taking of new births. In that verse, 'Sahāva' means 'together with'. 'Assa' refers to any one of those Stream-enterers mentioned as 'they do not take an eighth birth'. 'Dassanassampadāya' means the attainment of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). The Path of Stream-entry is called 'Vision' (dassana) because it is the very first vision of Nibbāna, having seen Nibbāna and fulfilled the necessary task. The manifestation of that Path-knowledge within oneself is 'attainment' (sampadā). Together with that attainment of vision, 'tayassu dhammā jahitā bhavanti' (three things are abandoned); here, the word 'su' is a mere functional particle (nipāta) used to complete the verse, as in the passage: 'Sāriputta, this great medicinal decoction of mine is in the food' (MN 1.156). Therefore, the meaning here is that as soon as that Stream-enterer is endowed with the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, three things are abandoned. Now, to show the abandoned things, he said: 'Sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchitañca, sīlabbataṃ vāpi yadatthi kiñci' (Personality belief, doubt, and whatever ritualistic practice there may be). In that phrase, 'Sakkāyadiṭṭhi' (personality belief) is the view with twenty bases regarding the 'body' (kāya) known as the five aggregates of clinging, which exists. Alternatively, it is the view regarding the body that exists, thus 'sakkāyadiṭṭhi'; meaning the view existing in the body of the aforementioned nature. Or, it is the view when the body exists; meaning the view that proceeds as 'the self is form (rūpa), etc.' when the body of the aforementioned nature exists. Because that personality belief is abandoned, all types of views are indeed abandoned, for it is their root. Wisdom is called 'cikicchita' (medical treatment) because it allays the disease of all defilements; that which is devoid of such medical treatment of wisdom, or that from which the medical treatment of wisdom is gone, is 'vicikicchita' (doubt), as in 'he doubts the Teacher', etc.
287:
This word (vicikicchita) is the name for the eightfold doubt as previously mentioned. Because that doubt has been abandoned, all doubts are abandoned, for that is their root. The practices and vows such as the cow-vow and dog-vow, which appear in passages like "Outside this Dispensation, recluses and brahmins are purified by habitual practices (sīla), purified by vows (vata)," are called "sīlabbata." Because that sīlabbata has been abandoned, all false practices such as nakedness and shaving the head are also abandoned, for that sīlabbata is their root. Therefore, at the very end of all, it is said, "Whatever (sīlabbata) there may be."

In this context, it should be understood that one abandons personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) by being endowed with the vision of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); one abandons doubt (vicikicchā) by being endowed with the vision of the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca); and one abandons wrong rites and rituals (sīlabbata) by being endowed with the vision of the truth of the path (magga-sacca) and the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca).

Having thus shown the abandonment of the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa) for that person, the Buddha now spoke the words, "And he is especially liberated from the four planes of misery," wishing to show that by abandoning the round of defilements, the round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa) that would have occurred is also abandoned. In that statement, the four planes of misery are hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, and the asura realm. The meaning is that even though this Stream-enterer may take rebirth for seven more lives, he is liberated from those four planes of misery.

Having thus shown the abandonment of the round of results for that person, the Buddha now spoke the words, "He is incapable of committing the six heinous crimes," wishing to show the abandonment of the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa), which is the root of this round of results. In that statement, "abhithāna" refers to heinous crimes. That person is incapable of committing those six crimes. Those crimes should be known as the acts mentioned in the Ekaka Nipāta such as, "Monks, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should deprive his mother of life," which include: matricide, patricide, killing an Arahant, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and following another teacher. In truth, a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) endowed with right view would not deprive even a termite or an ant of life; however, this was said to disparage the state of a worldling (puthujjana). Because a worldling is not endowed with right view, he may commit such heinous crimes. But a person endowed with vision (dassana-sampanna) is incapable of committing them. The use of the word "abhabba" (incapable) here is to show that they will not be committed even in future lives. Even if that person does not know in a future life that he is a noble disciple, by the very nature of things (dhammatā), he does not commit these six, or the five enmities such as killing along with following another teacher, making six points. Regarding this, some teachers read "chachābhithānāni." The example of children of noble disciples in a village handling dead fish etc. serves as an illustration here (noble children naturally avoid evil even without knowing).
288:
Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtue of the Gem of the Saṅgha by way of the distinguished qualities of the noble disciple—who, though still taking rebirth for seven lives, is superior to other persons who have not abandoned the taking of new existence—now utters the word of truth based on that very virtue: "Idam-pi saṅghe" (This too is in the Saṅgha). The meaning of that phrase should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. The authority of this verse is accepted by the non-human beings (deities and brahmas) residing in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

Thus, having spoken the truth based on the Saṅgha by way of the distinguished qualities of the person who will take rebirth for seven lives over those who have not abandoned new existence, the Buddha now began the verse starting with "Kiñcāpi so kammaṃ karoti pāpakaṃ" to speak of the virtue of the person endowed with vision who, even if living negligibly, does not conceal any committed fault, saying: "Not only is the person endowed with vision incapable of committing the six heinous crimes, but if he should commit even a slight evil deed, he is incapable of concealing it."

The meaning of that verse is: If that person endowed with vision, due to a lapse in mindfulness and living negligibly, should commit an evil deed with the body—excluding those worldly faults (lokavajja) which the Blessed One referred to when saying, "Whatever training rule I have prescribed for my disciples, my disciples will not transgress even for the sake of their lives," but committing other prescribed faults (paṇṇattivajja) such as those regarding hut-building (kuṭikāra) or sleeping in the same room (sahaseyya) which are loathed by the Buddha; or if he should commit an evil deed by speech such as reciting Dhamma word by word (padasodhamma), teaching Dhamma beyond five or six words to a woman (uttari-chappañcavācā), frivolous talk (samphappalāpa), or harsh speech (pharusavāca); or if he should commit an evil deed by mind such as the arising of greed or hatred, delighting in gold and silver, or lack of reflection in using robes and so on. That person is incapable of concealing that fault. Knowing "this is unallowable, this is not to be done," he does not conceal it even for a moment, but immediately reveals it to the Teacher or to wise fellow monks and amends it according to the Dhamma, or undertakes the restraint, saying, "I will not do it again." Why? Because it is said that for one who has seen the state (of Nibbāna), such incapacity exists. The meaning is that for a person endowed with vision who has seen the state of Nibbāna, it is said to be impossible to commit such an evil deed and then conceal it.

How so?
"Monks, just as a young, tender infant lying on his back, if he touches a hot coal with his hand or foot, quickly..."
289:
Just as (a child who steps on a glowing coal) quickly withdraws his foot, O monks, such is the nature (dhammatā) of a person endowed with vision (a Sotāpanna). Even if such a person commits an offense of such a nature that an emergence from it is known, he immediately confesses it, reveals it, and makes it clear to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life. Having confessed, revealed, and made it clear, he attains restraint in the future. (Majjhima Nikāya 1.496).

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of the Gem of the Saṅgha—specifically the quality of not concealing a committed fault even when a person endowed with vision lives negligently—now utters the word of truth beginning with "Idampi saṅghe" (This too in the Saṅgha) based on that very quality. The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. The authority of this verse is accepted by non-human beings, deities, and Brahmas in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

Thus, having spoken the truth based on the Saṅgha through various qualities of those included in the Saṅgha, the Blessed One, wishing to show the qualities of the Triple Gem, now begins to speak the truth based on the Buddha once more, relying on the scriptural Dhamma (Pariyatti Dhamma) taught briefly in this sutta and in detail in other suttas, starting with "Vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge" (Like a woodland thicket with blossoming tops). In that verse, a collection of trees situated close together is called "vana" (forest). A plant that grows with roots, heartwood, softwood, bark, branches, and leaves is called "gumba" or "pagumba". A thicket in the forest is called "vanappagumba". That very "vanappagumba" is expressed as "vanappagumbe". This can be said in this way, as in "savitakkasavicāre, avitakkavicāramatta, sukhe dukkhe jīve", etc. "Yathā" is a word of comparison (simile). "Phussitagga" means its tips are blossoming; it means flowers have bloomed on all branches and twigs. That term is expressed as "phussitagge" according to the previously mentioned method. Among the four months of summer, "the first month of summer" means—which month is it? It means the month of Citra (Tagu). That month is called "Paṭhamagimha" (First Summer) and also "Bālavassanta" (Early Spring). The meaning of the remaining words is clear.

The summary of the meaning here is: Just as in the early spring called the first summer, in a forest dense with various kinds of trees, a thicket—a term for a collection of young trees and bushes—with branches and tips in full bloom is exceedingly beautiful, even so, through the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana)...
290:
...through the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), right efforts (sammappadhāna), etc., or through the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), etc., and because it is exceedingly beautiful with the clusters of flowers that are the various distinctions of meaning, the excellent scriptural Dhamma (Pariyatti Dhamma) which leads to Nibbāna—because it shows the path leading to Nibbāna—was taught not for the sake of gain and offerings, nor for the sake of desiring respect and honor, but indeed, with a heart moved by great compassion (mahākaruṇā), He taught it for the supreme benefit of beings. In this word "paramanhitāya", the inclusion of the nasal (niggahīta) in "paraman" is for the sake of metrical ease in the verse, but the meaning is "He taught for the sake of Nibbāna, which is the supreme benefit".

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of this scriptural Dhamma which is like a woodland thicket with well-blossomed tips and branches, now utters the word of truth centered on the Buddha, based on that very scriptural Dhamma, starting with "Idampi buddhe" (This too in the Buddha). The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. However, it should be connected and understood that this excellent gem, known as the scriptural Dhamma of the aforementioned nature, exists in the Buddha. The authority of this verse is accepted by non-human beings living in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken the truth centered on the Buddha through the scriptural Dhamma, now begins to speak through the supramundane Dhamma (Lokuttara Dhamma) with the verse starting "Varo varညူ" (The Excellent One, the Knower of the Excellent). In that verse, "Varo" (Excellent) is so called because He is desired by noble persons with an inclination toward the sublime Dhamma, thinking, "Oh, would that we too were of such a nature!", or because He is endowed with excellent qualities; it means supreme or most noble. "Varaññū" means the Knower of Nibbāna. Nibbāna is "vara" (excellent) in the sense of being supreme among all dhammas. And the Blessed One realized and knew that excellent Nibbāna by Himself at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "Varado" (Giver of the Excellent) means He gives the excellent Dhamma—either the part pertaining to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) or the part pertaining to the cultivation of latent tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya)—to the group of five (pañcavaggiya), the group of thirty (bhaddavaggiya), the matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila), and other devas and humans. "Varāharo" (Bringer of the Excellent) is so called because He brought the excellent Path (magga). For the Blessed One, starting from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, fulfilling the thirty perfections, brought the ancient excellent Path followed by previous Fully Enlightened Buddhas; therefore, He is called "Varāharo". Furthermore, He is "Varo" because of the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa); "Varaññū" because of the realization of Nibbāna; "Varado" because of giving the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha) to beings; and "Varāharo" because of bringing the supreme practice. Because there is no one superior to Him in these supramundane qualities, He is called "Anuttaro" (Peerless).

Another way: He is "Varo" through the fulfillment of the foundation of peace (upasama-adhiṭṭhāna); "Varaññū" through the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom (paññā-adhiṭṭhāna); "Varado" through the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity (cāga-adhiṭṭhāna); and "Varāharo" through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth (sacca-adhiṭṭhāna). He brought the excellent Truth of the Path. Likewise, He is "Varo" due to the accumulation of merit; "Varaññū" due to the accumulation of wisdom; and "Varado" because He grants the means for attaining Buddhahood to those who desire it.
291:
The Blessed One is called 'Varāharo' (Bringer of the Excellent) because he brings the excellent means for those who desire the state of a Paccekabuddha. He is called 'Anuttaro' (Unsurpassed) because he is peerless in various respects. Alternatively, he is called 'Ācariya' (Teacher) because he became a teacher to others without having a teacher himself. It is said, 'Dhammavaraṃ adesayi' (He taught the excellent Dhamma) because he taught the noble Dhamma, endowed with qualities such as being well-expounded (svākkhāta), for the benefit of those who desire the state of a disciple. The rest is as previously explained.

Thus, having declared his own qualities through the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), the Blessed One now performs an act of truth (sacca-vacana) centered on the Buddha, based on those very qualities, starting with "Idampi Buddhe" (This too in the Buddha). The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. Specifically, it should be connected thus: "This noble ninefold supramundane Dhamma which the Buddha realized, which he gave, which he brought, and which he taught—this too is a precious jewel in the Buddha."

The authority of this verse was accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) in a hundred thousand million world systems.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken the truth centered on the Buddha with two verses based on the Pariyatti Dhamma and the Supramundane Dhamma, now begins to speak the truth centered on the Saṅgha, based on the quality of attaining Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna) by those individuals who heard that Pariyatti Dhamma, practiced according to what they heard, and attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. He begins with "Khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ" (The old is exhausted). In that verse, 'khīṇaṃ' means well-severed. 'Purāṇaṃ' means old kamma. 'Navaṃ' means kamma being created presently. 'Natthi sambhavaṃ' means the absence of the manifestation of arising. 'Virattacittā' means those with minds detached from lust. 'Āyatike bhavasmiṃ' means in a future existence. 'Te' refers to those taintless monks (khīṇāsava bhikkhus) whose old kamma is exhausted, for whom there is no new arising, and who are detached from future existence. 'Khīṇabījā' means those whose seeds of kamma are severed. 'Avirūḷhichandā' means those devoid of the desire for further growth. 'Nibbanti' means they are extinguished. 'Dhīrā' means those endowed with wisdom. 'Yathāyaṃ padīpo' means just like this lamp.

What is meant is this: For beings, the old kamma of the past, though it has arisen and ceased, is not yet exhausted in its ability to bring about rebirth because the moisture of craving (taṇhā-sineha) has not been abandoned. For those Arahants, that old kamma is exhausted in its inability to give results in the future, like a seed burnt by fire, because the moisture of craving has been dried up by the Path of Arahantship. And for those Arahants, the kamma called 'new' which is presently occurring by way of Buddha-worship and so on, has no possibility of arising to give results in the future, like the flower of a tree whose roots are severed, precisely because of the abandoning of craving. Those who have minds detached from future existence due to the abandoning of craving—those taintless monks—for whom "Kamma is the field..."
292:
"...consciousness is the seed" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.77). Because the rebirth-consciousness mentioned here is exhausted due to the exhaustion of kamma, they are 'khīṇabījā' (those whose seeds are exhausted).

The desire (chanda) that previously existed for growth (virūḷhi) known as renewed existence (punabbhava) has been abandoned by the abandoning of the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca); thus, because there is no arising at the time of death as there was before, they are 'avirūḷhichandā' (those without desire for growth). Being endowed with wisdom, they are 'dhīrā' (the wise). With the cessation of the final consciousness (carima-viññāṇa), they are extinguished just as this lamp is extinguished. Furthermore, they transcend the path of designation such as "beings with form" or "formless beings."

At that time, among the lamps lit to honor the city deities, one lamp went out. Wishing to point that out, the Buddha said, "Yathāyaṃ padīpo" (Just as this lamp).

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of attaining Nibbāna without remainder by those individuals who heard the Pariyatti Dhamma taught in the previous two verses, practiced according to what they heard, and attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, now concludes the teaching by performing an act of truth centered on the Saṅgha, based on that very quality, starting with "Idampi Saṅghe" (This too in the Saṅgha). The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. Specifically, it should be connected thus: "This precious jewel in the Saṅgha, known as the Nibbāna of the taintless monks in the manner described, is excellent."

The authority of this verse was also accepted with applause by the devas and brahmas in a hundred thousand million world systems.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the royal family attained well-being. All calamities were subsided. Eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma.

239-241. Then Sakka, the king of devas, thought: "The Blessed One has brought well-being to the citizens by performing acts of truth based on the qualities of the Triple Gem. I, too, should say something based on the qualities of the Triple Gem for the sake of the citizens' well-being." Having thought thus, he recited three verses at the end, starting with "Yānīdha bhūtāni" (Whatever beings are gathered here). In those verses, he is called 'Tathāgata' because he has come (āgata) just as those who strive for the welfare of the world should come; or because he has gone (gata) as they should go; or because he has known (ājānana) as they should know; or because he knows (jānana) as one should know; and because he speaks (gadana) that which is truly so (tatha).

And because he is greatly honored by devas and humans with external requisites such as flowers and scents, and with internal practice such as the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhamma-anudhamma-paṭipatti), Sakka, the king of devas, together with his entire host of devas...
293:
Sakka, the King of Devas, gathered the celestial assembly and said: "We salute the Buddha, the Tathāgata, honored by gods and humans; may there be safety."

Because the Path-Dhamma (magga-dhamma) goes to Nibbāna by completely cutting off the host of defilements through the power of calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā) joined in a yoke, it is called "Tathāgata" (Thus Gone). The Dhamma of Nibbāna is also realized through wisdom as it truly is; it is perfectly conducive to the destruction of all suffering. Since the Buddhas and other noble ones have understood it thus without deviation, it is called "Tathāgata." Because the Saṅgha also has reached the goal through the various paths as those practicing for their own benefit should, it is likewise called "Tathāgata." Therefore, in the remaining two verses, it is said: "We salute the Tathāgata Dhamma; may there be safety," and "We salute the Tathāgata Saṅgha; may there be safety." The rest of the explanation is as previously stated.

Thus, Sakka, the King of Devas, having recited these three verses, circumambulated the Blessed One and returned to the celestial city with his retinue of devas. The Blessed One preached that same Ratana Sutta on the second day as well, and again eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). In this way, the Blessed One preached until the seventh day, and every day there was a similar realization of the Dhamma. The Blessed One stayed in Vesālī for half a month (fifteen days) and then informed the kings, saying, "We shall depart." Then the kings, with double the honors, escorted the Blessed One to the banks of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) over three days.

The Nāga kings living in the Ganges thought: "Humans are paying honor to the Tathāgata Buddha; why should we not do the same?" Having thought so, they created boats made of gold, silver, and gems, arranged thrones of gold, silver, and gems, and covered the surface of the water with five-colored lotuses. They approached the Blessed One, saying, "Please show us favor." The Blessed One accepted and boarded a jewel-boat, and the five hundred monks boarded their respective boats. The Nāga kings led the Blessed One and the Saṅgha to the Nāga realm. There, it is said, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the Nāga assembly throughout the night. On the second day, they offered a great gift of celestial food and drink. After giving the blessing of appreciation (anumodanā), the Blessed One departed from the Nāga realm.

The terrestrial devas also thought: "Humans and Nāgas are paying honor to the Tathāgata Buddha; why should we not do the same?" and they raised tiered umbrellas in the forests, trees, and mountains. In this manner, up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm...
294:
...a special and great honor arose. King Bimbisāra also performed double the honors that were given when the Licchavī kings arrived. In the same manner as previously described, he escorted the Blessed One to Rājagaha in five days.

After the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagaha, following the meal, a conversation arose among the monks who had gathered in the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla): "Oh, how wonderful is the power of the Buddha, the Blessed One! For his sake, the ground for eight yojanas on both sides of the Ganges was leveled, strewn with sand, and beautifully covered with flowers. The water of the Ganges for one yojana was covered with lotuses of various colors. Tiered umbrellas were raised all the way up to the Akaniṭṭha realm." The Blessed One, knowing the subject of their conversation, emerged from the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi) and, proceeding with a psychic power suitable for the moment, sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the circular pavilion. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" The monks related everything to him. The Blessed One said: "Monks, this special honor did not arise through my power as a Buddha, nor through the power of Nāgas, Devas, or Brahmas. Rather, it arose through the power of a small act of giving in a past life." The monks said: "Venerable Sir, we do not know of that small act of giving. May the Blessed One please tell us about it so that we may know."

The Blessed One said: Monks, in the past, there was a Brahmin named Saṅkha in the city of Takkasilā. He had a son, a youth named Susīma, who was about sixteen years of age. One day, the youth Susīma approached his father, paid respects, and stood to one side. The father asked, "What is it, dear Susīma?" He replied, "Father, I wish to go to Vārāṇasī to learn the arts." "In that case, dear Susīma, a certain Brahmin of such a name is my friend; go to him and learn," he said, and gave him a thousand kahāpaṇas. Taking the money, Susīma paid respects to his parents and eventually reached Vārāṇasī. He approached the teacher in the proper manner, paid respects, and introduced himself. The teacher, thinking "He is the son of my friend," accepted the youth and provided him with all hospitality. After the youth had recovered from the fatigue of the journey, he placed the thousand kahāpaṇas at the teacher's feet and requested permission to learn the arts. The teacher granted permission and began to teach him.
295:
The youth Susīma learned quickly and extensively, retaining all the knowledge he acquired without loss, like lion's oil kept in a golden vessel. Thus, he completed the studies that usually take twelve years in just a few months. When he recited his lessons, he could see only the beginning and the middle, but not the end. He then approached his teacher and said, "I see only the beginning and the middle of this science, but I do not see the end." The teacher replied, "Dear son, it is the same for me." "Teacher, then who knows the end of this science?" he asked. "Dear son, there are sages (Paccekabuddhas) in Isipatana; they would know," the teacher said. "Teacher, I will approach them and ask," he said. "Dear son, ask as you wish," the teacher replied.

The youth went to Isipatana, approached the Paccekabuddhas, and asked, "Do you know the beginning, the middle, and the end?" "Yes, lay devotee, we know," they replied. "Please teach that end to me as well," he requested. "Lay devotee, if so, you must ordain; it is not possible to learn it without ordaining," they said. "Venerable sirs, very well, please ordain me, or have me do whatever you wish so that I may know the end of the Dhamma," he requested. After ordaining him, as they were not yet able to engage him in meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), they taught him the training of proper conduct (abhisamācārika), such as how to dress and how to robe himself. While practicing those trainings, because he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), he realized the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (paccekabodhiñāṇa) before long. He became famous throughout Bārāṇasī as "Susīma Paccekabuddha," endowed with the highest gains, fame, and followers. Due to having performed past kamma that leads to a short life, he attained Parinibbāna not long after. The Paccekabuddhas and the great multitude performed the funeral rites, took the relics, and established a stupa at the city gate.

Then, the Brahmin Saṅkha, thinking, "It has been a long time since my son left, and I have no news of him," wished to see his son and set out from Takkasilā, eventually reaching Bārāṇasī. Seeing a large gathering of people, he thought, "Surely among so many people, someone will know news of my son." He approached them and asked, "Has a youth named Susīma come here? Do you know any news of him?" They replied, "Yes, Brahmin, we know. He became a master of the three Vedas under a Brahmin in this city, then ordained under the Paccekabuddhas, became a Paccekabuddha himself, and attained Parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). This is the stupa established for him." He [fell] to the ground...
296: (The brahmin Saṅkha,) having struck the ground with his hands and wept and lamented, went to the courtyard of that shrine, pulled up the grass, brought sand in his upper garment, and scattered it in the courtyard of the Paccekabuddha's shrine. Then, sprinkling the ground all around with water from a water-pot, he made an offering of wild flowers, raised a banner with his upper garment, fastened his own umbrella over the shrine, and departed. Thus, having shown the past story, he connected that Jātaka with the present and preached a Dhamma discourse to the monks: "Monks, it might occur to you that the brahmin named Saṅkha at that time was someone else. It should not be seen in this way; I myself was the brahmin Saṅkha at that time. I pulled up the grass in the courtyard of the shrine of the Paccekabuddha Susīma; as a result of that kamma, they made the eight-league road level and clean, free from stumps and thorns. I scattered sand at that shrine; as a result of that, they scattered sand on the eight-league road. I made an offering of wild flowers at that shrine; as a result of that, they spread a carpet of various flowers on both land and water along the nine-league road. I sprinkled the ground with water from a water-pot at that shrine; as a result of that, a pokkharavassa rain fell in the city of Vesālī. I raised a banner and fastened an umbrella at that shrine; as a result of that, banners were raised and umbrellas upon umbrellas were hoisted as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm. Thus, monks, this extraordinary honor paid to me did not arise through the power of a Buddha, nor through the power of nāgas, devas, or Brahmās; rather, it arose through the power of a small sacrifice." At the end of the Dhamma discourse, he spoke this verse: "If, by giving up a small pleasure, one sees a great happiness, the wise person should give up the small pleasure, seeing the great happiness." ## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā, ## the explanation of the Ratana Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
297:
## 2. Commentary on the Āmagandha Sutta

This sutta, beginning with "Sāmāka, ciṅgūlaka, cīnaka," and so forth, is the Āmagandha Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising? Before the Blessed One had appeared in the world, a Brahmin named Āmagandha, together with five hundred young students, went forth as hermits. Having entered the Himalayas, they had a hermitage built in a mountain valley and lived there, subsisting only on forest roots and fruits; they never ate fish or meat. At that time, because those hermits did not consume salt, sour foods, and the like, they developed jaundice (paṇḍuroga). Therefore, those hermits thought, "Let us go to the human settlements to consume salt, sour foods, and such," and they arrived at a border village. There, the people, being inspired by the hermits, invited and fed them. After the hermits had finished their meal, the people brought them couches, stools, utensils, foot oil, and other necessities, saying, "Venerable sirs, please stay here; do not be weary," and after showing them a place to stay, they departed. On the second day, they again gave offerings to the hermits, and subsequently, they provided offerings day by day, house by house in succession.

After staying there for four months and consuming salt, sour foods, and so forth, the hermits' bodies became strong. They then informed the people, "Lay followers, we shall depart." The people gave them oil, rice, and other provisions. Taking those supplies, the hermits returned to their own hermitage. They continued to come to that village in the same manner year after year. The people, knowing the time of the hermits' arrival, would stay prepared with rice and other items for the offering, and when the hermits arrived, they would attend to them well in the same way.

Then the Blessed One appeared in the world, and after setting the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he eventually went to Sāvatthī and resided there. Seeing the fulfillment of the spiritual potential (upanissaya) of those hermits, he set out from there, surrounded by the community of monks, and while wandering on tour, he eventually reached that village. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the people made great offerings. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to them. Through that Dhamma teaching, some became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmi), some Non-returners (Anāgāmi), and some went forth and attained Arahantship. The Blessed One then returned to Sāvatthī.

Later, those hermits arrived at that village. Although the people saw the hermits, they did not show the same great excitement and joy as before. The hermits asked about the reason: "Lay followers, why are these people not as they were before? Is this village troubled by royal punishment, or by famine, or has some monk more endowed with virtues like morality than us arrived at this village?" The people replied, "Venerable sirs, this village is not troubled by royal punishment, nor by famine; rather, the Buddha..."
298:
