"...has appeared in the world, and that Blessed One, preaching the Dhamma for the benefit of many, has come to this place," (so the people said).

Hearing those words, the hermit Āmagandha asked, "O householders, did you say 'Buddha'?" "Venerable sir, we said 'Buddha'," they replied, saying it three times. Then, with a joyful mind and uttering words of delight, he said, "Even this sound 'Buddha' is rare in the world," and he asked, "Does that Buddha eat āmagandha, or does he not?" When asked, "Venerable hermit, what is called āmagandha?" he replied, "O householders, āmagandha means fish and meat." The people said, "Venerable hermit, the Blessed One consumes fish and meat." Hearing this, the hermit became displeased. He thought, "Indeed, he might not be the Buddha." Then he thought again, "The appearance of Buddhas is rare; I will go, see the Buddha, ask him, and find out." Then, asking the people for the way the Blessed One had gone, he traveled in great haste like a cow yearning for its calf, staying only one night at each place along the entire journey, until he reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jetavana monastery with his followers. At that time, the Blessed One was already sitting on the seat for the purpose of preaching the Dhamma. The hermits approached the Blessed One and, remaining silent and without bowing, sat down at one side. The Blessed One greeted them in a friendly manner, saying, "O hermits, is it bearable for you?" and so forth. They also replied, "It is bearable, Master Gotama," and so on. Then the hermit Āmagandha asked the Blessed One, "Master Gotama, do you eat āmagandha, or do you not?" When asked, "Brahmin, what is this that is called āmagandha?" he replied, "Master Gotama, it is fish and meat." The Blessed One said, "Brahmin, fish and meat are not what is called āmagandha. Rather, all defilements and evil unwholesome states are what is called āmagandha." He continued, "Brahmin, it is not only you who asks about āmagandha now; in the past also, a Brahmin named Tissa asked the Blessed One Kassapa. That Brahmin asked in this way, and the Blessed One answered him in this way." Thus, bringing forth the verses spoken by the Brahmin Tissa and the Blessed One Kassapa, and making the Brahmin understand through those verses, he said, "Sāmāka, ciṅgūlaka, cīnaka," and so forth. This is the origin of this sutta in this context.

In the past, it is said that the Bodhisatta Kassapa, having fulfilled the perfections for eight incalculable periods (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons, took rebirth in the womb of a Brahmin woman named Dhanavatī, the wife of the Brahmin Brahmadatta, in the city of Bārāṇasī. The Chief Disciple also passed away from the deva world on that very day and was reborn in the womb of the wife of the deputy chaplain Brahmin (anupurohita). Thus, on the same day...
299:
Conception and birth occurred on the very same day for both Kassapa and Tissa. One was named Kassapa and the other Tissa. These two friends, who were childhood playmates, grew up in due course. Tissa’s father urged his son, saying, "Dear Tissa, this Kassapa will renounce the world, ordain, and become a Buddha. You too should ordain in his presence and make an end of the suffering of saṃsāra." Tissa agreed, went to the Bodhisatta, and said, "Friend, let us both ordain." The Bodhisatta also agreed.

Later, when they reached adulthood, Tissa again said to the Bodhisatta, "Come, friend, let us ordain," but the Bodhisatta did not yet renounce the world. Thinking, "His wisdom is not yet mature," Tissa renounced the world on his own, became an ascetic (isi), and lived in a hermitage he built at the foot of a mountain in the forest. Later, while still living at home, the Bodhisatta practiced mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), developed the four jhānas and the supernormal powers (abhiññā), and then traveled by palace to the vicinity of the Bodhimaṇḍa. He made a resolution, "May this palace return to its original place," and it returned to its place. It is said that one cannot approach the Bodhimaṇḍa without ordaining. Having ordained and reached the Bodhimaṇḍa, the Bodhisatta sat down and practiced supreme effort for seven days, and on the seventh day, he realized the Perfect Self-Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi).

At that time, twenty thousand ordained monks were living in the Isipatana forest. Then, the Blessed One Kassapa addressed them and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). At the end of the discourse, all of them became Arahants. The Blessed One lived there in the Isipatana forest, surrounded by twenty thousand monks. King Kikī, the King of Kāsī, attended to the Blessed One with the four requisites.

Then one day, a man living in Bārāṇasī, while searching for sandalwood and other things on the mountain, reached the hermitage of the ascetic Tissa. He paid homage to the ascetic and stood in a suitable place. Seeing the man, the ascetic asked, "Where have you come from?" "I have come from Bārāṇasī, venerable sir," he replied. "What is the news there?" he asked. "Venerable sir, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha named Kassapa has appeared there," he replied. Hearing those words, which are rare to hear, the ascetic was filled with joy and asked, "Does that Buddha eat āmagandha or not?" "Venerable sir, what is āmagandha?" the man asked. "Friend, it is fish and meat," he said. "Venerable sir, the Blessed One does eat fish and meat," he replied. Hearing this, the ascetic became displeased and thought again, "I will go and ask that Buddha. If he says, 'I consume āmagandha,' then I will restrain him, saying, 'Venerable sir, this is not suitable for your birth, family, and lineage,' and then I will ordain in his presence and make an end of the suffering of saṃsāra." Thus he quickly planned.
300: Taking his requisites and staying only one night at each place along the journey, he arrived at Bārāṇasī in the evening and entered Isipatana. At that time, the Blessed One was already seated on his seat to preach the Dhamma. That ascetic approached the Blessed One and, without paying homage, stood silently in a suitable place. Seeing that ascetic, the Blessed One greeted him in the same manner as previously mentioned. The ascetic also said, "Is it bearable, Master Kassapa?" and so on, and sat in a suitable place, then asked the Blessed One: "Master Kassapa, do you eat āmagandha, or do you not?" "Brahmin, I do not eat āmagandha," he replied. "Excellent, excellent, Master Kassapa! By not eating āmagandha, you have done a good thing. This is fitting for Master Kassapa's birth, family, and lineage." Then the Blessed One thought: "Although I say 'I do not eat āmagandha' referring to the defilements, this brahmin believes and perceives only fish and meat as āmagandha. Tomorrow, instead of entering the village for alms, I will consume the alms-food brought from King Kikī's palace. By doing so, a conversation will arise concerning āmagandha. Then I will make this ascetic understand through a Dhamma teaching." Having planned this, early on the second day, after attending to his body, he entered the Gandhakuṭi. When the monks saw the door of the Gandhakuṭi closed, they knew, "The Blessed One does not wish to go out with the monks today," and after circumambulating the Gandhakuṭi, they went for alms. The Blessed One also came out of the Gandhakuṭi and sat on the prepared seat. The ascetic, after cooking and eating leaf-broth, sat near the Blessed One. King Kikī of Kāsi, seeing the monks wandering for alms, asked, "Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One?" Hearing that he was at the monastery, he sent food endowed with various flavors and many kinds of meat to the Blessed One. The ministers took it to the monastery, informed the Blessed One, and after offering the water of donation, served him. First, they offered gruel endowed with various kinds of meat. Seeing this, the ascetic stood watching, thinking, "Will he eat it or not?" While the ascetic was watching, the Blessed One drank the gruel and put a piece of meat into his mouth. Seeing this, the ascetic became angry. Again, after the gruel was finished, they offered food with various flavors; seeing him eat that too, he became extremely angry, thinking, "While eating fish and meat, he says 'I do not eat it'!" Then, approaching the Blessed One who was sitting after finishing his meal and washing his hands and feet, he said: "Master Kassapa, you speak falsely. This is not the act of a wise man. Falsehood is censured by the Buddhas. Even those ascetics living at the foot of mountains, subsisting on wild roots and fruits, do not speak falsely." Praising the virtues of the ascetics with a verse, he said: ## Sāmāka, ciṅgūlaka, and cīnaka grains...
301:
In those verses, *sāmāka* refers to types of wild millet collected by shaking or selecting the ears. Similarly, *ciṅgūlaka* have ears shaped like *kaṇavīra* (oleander) flowers. *Cīnaka* refers to wild beans that grow naturally at the foot of mountains in the forest without being planted. *Pattapphala* refers to any kind of green leaf. *Mūlapphala* refers to any kind of root or tuber. *Gavipphala* refers to any kind of fruit from trees or creepers. Alternatively, by the word *mūla*, roots and tubers should be understood; by the word *phala*, fruits from trees and creepers; and by the word *gavipphala*, fruits grown in water such as water chestnuts (*siṅghāṭaka*) and *kaseru* tubers. *Dhammena laddha* means food obtained by wandering for alms in the forest, having abandoned wrong livelihoods such as acting as a messenger. *Sataṃ* refers to the Noble Ones (*ariyas*). *Asnamānā* means consuming or eating.

'Those who do not desire sense pleasures do not speak falsehood' means that those Noble Ones, the ascetics who eat those wild grains like *sāmāka* without the attachment of 'this is mine,' do not speak falsehood. This is in contrast to the Venerable Kassapa, who, while desiring sense pleasures such as delicious tastes and eating the 'stench' (*āmagandha*) of meat, says, 'I do not eat the stench,' thereby speaking falsehood. Thus, by praising the ascetics, he shows his disparagement of the Blessed One.

Having disparaged the Blessed One by means of praising the ascetics, he now shows the grounds for disparagement he intends, and wishing to disparage the Blessed One directly, he says the words beginning with '*Yadasnamāno*.' In that context, the letter 'd' is a phonetic euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). The meaning is: eating any kind of meat, such as rabbit or partridge, which is well-prepared through preliminary processes like washing and cutting, and well-finished through subsequent processes like cooking and seasoning with spices; not prepared by parents, but given by others who love the Dhamma and consider, 'This person is worthy of offerings'; offered with respect, excellent and well-adorned; excellent because of its superior taste, nutritional essence, and ability to provide strength and vigor. Not only eating just any meat, but also consuming this fine rice meal made of selected *sāli* rice grains free from black specks. 'Kassapa, you eat the stench (*āmagandha*); while eating any kind of meat and consuming this fine rice, you eat the stench, Kassapa.' Thus, he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name.

Having disparaged the Blessed One regarding food, he now disparages him by accusing him of lying, saying the words beginning with '*Na āmagandho... pe... susaṅkhatehi*.'
302:
The meaning of that verse is: 'Previously, when I asked, you said, "The stench (*āmagandha*) is not suitable for me." You spoke in this way quite definitely, you pseudo-brahmin (*brahmabandhu*), who are a brahmin by birth alone, devoid of brahminical virtues.' This is said as a reproach. *Sālinamannaṃ* means rice cooked from fine *sāli* rice. *Paribhuñjamāno* means while eating. *Sakuntamaṃsehi susaṅkhatehi* refers to the well-prepared bird meat that was offered to the Blessed One at that time.

Even while speaking thus, he looked at the Blessed One's body from the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair and saw the perfection of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks, as well as the fathom-wide aura surrounding him. Then he thought, "A person with a body adorned with such marks of a Great Man is not worthy of speaking falsehood. Indeed, this *uṇṇā* hair born between the eyebrows, white and soft like a tuft of cotton, and the fact that only one hair grows in each pore, are the results of speaking truthful words in a previous life. How then could he speak falsehood now? Surely, there must be another kind of 'stench' (*āmagandha*) that he was referring to when he said, 'Brahmin, I do not eat the stench.' What if I were to ask him about this?" Having thought this, and with great respect and devotion arising, he addressed him by his clan name and spoke the remainder of the verse:

"I ask you this matter, Kassapa: of what nature is your 'stench' (*āmagandha*)?"

Then, to explain the meaning of *āmagandha*, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "*Pāṇātipāto*." In that context, *pāṇātipāto* means the killing of living beings. In the phrase *vadha-cheda-bandhanaṃ*, *vadha* means beating beings with sticks and so on; *cheda* means cutting off hands, feet, and so on; *bandhanaṃ* means binding with ropes and so on. *Theyyaṃ musāvādo* means stealing and speaking falsehood. *Nikati* means fraud—creating hope by saying "I will give, I will do" and then frustrating that hope. *Vañcanāni* means deceptions, such as making someone take what is not gold as gold. *Ajjhenakuttaṃ* means the useless study of various texts. *Paradārasevanā* means committing misconduct with the wives of others. "This is the stench (*āmagandha*), not the eating of meat; indeed, the practice of these unwholesome states such as killing is what is called the stench."
303: Āmagandha (the stench of raw flesh/defilement) means the smell of rot, the smell of a decaying corpse. Why? Because it is unpleasant, mixed with the impurities of defilements (kilesa), loathed by the virtuous, and brings about a supreme foul odor. Beings with abundant defilements have a very foul odor because of those defilements. For those free from defilements, even their dead body does not emit a foul odor. Therefore, only these defilements are called āmagandha. As for eating meat, if it is not seen, heard, or suspected (to have been killed specifically for oneself), it is blameless. Therefore, eating meat is not āmagandha. Having thus answered regarding āmagandha in one way through the teaching based on principles (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), now, because various beings are possessed of various types of āmagandha (defilements)—not one being with all, nor all beings with only one—the Buddha, wishing to reveal those various types of āmagandha to them, spoke two verses through the teaching based on persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), starting with 'Ye idha kāmesu asaññatā janā'. In that verse, 'Ye idha kāmesu asaññatā janā' refers to those ordinary people (puthujjana) in this world who are unrestrained due to a lack of self-control and boundaries in sensual pleasures (kāma), even regarding mothers, maternal aunts, and so on. 'Rasesu giddhā' refers to those who are greedy, attached, infatuated, and obsessed with tastes cognizable by the tongue, consuming them without seeing the danger and without the wisdom for liberation from saṃsāra. 'Asucibhāvamassitā' refers to those who, due to that greed for taste, resort to various types of impure states known as wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) to obtain those tastes. 'Natthikadiṭṭhī' refers to those possessed of the ten types of wrong view, such as 'there is no result of giving'. 'Visamā' refers to those possessed of unrighteous (uneven) bodily actions and so forth. 'Durannayā' refers to those who are difficult to guide, who wrongly cling to their own views, and who are hard to make relinquish their misconceptions. 'Esāmagandho' refers to the six types of āmagandha indicated in this verse based on the person: 'unrestraint in sensual pleasures, greed for taste, failure in livelihood, nihilistic view, unrighteousness such as bodily misconduct, and being difficult to guide,' as previously explained. 'Na hi maṃsabhojanaṃ' means that eating meat, in the sense already stated, is not āmagandha. In the second verse, 'Ye lūkhasā' means those who are harsh and tasteless, devoted to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga). 'Dāruṇā' means those who are cruel and harsh due to being difficult to admonish.
304: 'Piṭṭhimaṃsikā' refers to those who speak sweetly in one's presence but speak ill behind one's back. Because they are unable to look one in the face and are like those who eat the flesh of the back in one's absence, they are called 'piṭṭhimaṃsikā' (backbiters). 'Mittadduno' refers to those who betray friends. It means those who act wrongly toward friends who trust them with their wives, wealth, and lives. 'Nikkaruṇā' refers to those who are devoid of compassion and desire the harm of beings. 'Atimānino' refers to those possessed of extreme conceit, as described in the Vibhaṅga: 'Here, someone despises others because of birth... or some other ground; such conceit and the mind's desire for self-exaltation is called atimāna.' 'Adānasīlā' refers to those who are uncharitable by nature, not inclined toward giving, and not delighting in sharing. 'Na ca denti kassaci' means that because of that uncharitable nature, they do not give anything to anyone even when asked. They are like people in families that have never given before, destined for the state of hungry ghosts (peta) parched by craving. Some teachers read 'ādānasīlā', meaning those who have the habit of only taking and do not give anything to anyone. 'This is āmagandha (stench); eating meat is not āmagandha.' Through this verse, based on the person, the eight types of āmagandha should be understood as previously stated: 'harshness, cruelty, backbiting, betrayal of friends, pitilessness, extreme conceit, uncharitableness, and not giving.' Eating meat is not āmagandha. Having thus spoken two verses through the teaching based on persons, and knowing that the inclination of that ascetic (tāpasa) had changed, the Buddha spoke one verse through the teaching based on principles (dhammādhiṭṭhāna). In that verse, 'kodho' (anger) should be understood in the same way as stated in the Uraga Sutta. 'Mado' (intoxication/pride) is the state of the mind's intoxication in various forms as explained in the Vibhaṅga, such as 'intoxication with birth, intoxication with lineage, intoxication with health,' and so on. 'Thambho' is the state of obstinacy. 'Paccupaṭṭhāpanā' means standing in opposition; it refers to standing in resistance to the method explained according to the Dhamma. 'Māyā' is the nature of wishing to conceal the sins one has committed, as analyzed in the Vibhaṅga: 'Here, someone having committed misconduct by body...' and so on. 'Usūyā' is envy (issā) regarding the gains and honor of others. 'Bhassasumussayo' means exalted talk, referring to the nature of self-exaltation. 'Mānātimāno' refers to conceit and over-conceit: 'Here, someone, because of birth... or some other ground, previously...'
305:
One regards oneself as equal to others; subsequently, one regards oneself as superior; one regards others as inferior. Such conceit... is analyzed in the Vibhaṅga as 'the banner of the mind,' the state of desiring prominence. 'Asabbhi santhavo' means association with the unrighteous (asappurisa). 'This is āmagandha, not the eating of meat' means that this ninefold mass of unwholesome states, beginning with anger, should be understood as āmagandha in the sense previously stated, and not the eating of meat.

Having thus shown the ninefold āmagandha through the teaching based on dhammas (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), the Buddha, wishing to explain āmagandha again through the teaching based on persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) in the manner previously mentioned, spoke three verses. In those verses, 'ye pāpasīlā' refers to those who are well-known in the world as 'evil-natured' because of their evil conduct. 'Iṇaghātasūcakā' refers to those who, in the manner stated in the Vasala Sutta, take the debts of others and, not wishing to repay, destroy the debt, as well as those who are backbiters through slander. 'Vohārakūṭā idha pāṭirūpikā' refers to those who, in this context, while standing in the place of judgment, take bribes and cause the rightful owners to lose, being endowed with fraudulent judgment; thus they are called 'vohārakūṭā' (fraudulent in trade/judgment). They are called 'pāṭirūpikā' because they counterfeit the appearance of being established in Dhamma. Alternatively, 'idha' means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Pāṭirūpikā' refers to immoral monks. Because they have an appearance similar to the virtuous through the perfection of their deportment and so forth, they are called 'paṭirūpa'; 'paṭirūpa' itself is 'pāṭirūpika.' 'Narādhamā yedha karonti kibbisam' means those vile men in this world who commit disgusting deeds, which are called wrong practices, toward their parents, or toward the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and so forth. 'This is āmagandha, not the eating of meat' means that the sixfold āmagandha shown by this verse based on persons—namely, evil-naturedness (pāpasīlatā), debt-destruction (iṇaghātatā), backbiting (sūcakatā), fraudulent judgment (vohārakūṭatā), hypocrisy (pāṭirūpikatā), and the commission of vile deeds (kibbisakāritā)—should be understood in the sense previously stated, and not the eating of meat.

'Ye idha pāṇesu asaññatā janā' means those people in this world who, because they act according to their desires toward living beings, killing even hundreds or thousands without even a trace of compassion, are called 'unrestrained' (asaññata). 'Paresamādāya vihesamuyyutā' means those who take the property, wealth, or life belonging to others and, after taking it, exert themselves in harming those who are pleading or forbidding them with their palms, clods of earth, sticks, and so forth. Or, it means those who capture other beings and, having undertaken to kill 'ten today, twenty today,' exert themselves in harming them through slaughter, binding, and so forth. 'Dussīlaluddā' means those who are immoral and cruel...
306:
Because of evil conduct, cruelty, ruthless actions, and hands stained with blood, fishermen, hunters, fowlers, and the like are intended here. 'Pharusa' means harsh speech. 'Anādara' means being devoid of regard, lacking the mindful thought, 'I will not do such a thing now; I will refrain from this.' 'This alone is āmagandha; the eating of meat is not āmagandha'—this is pointed out based on persons through this verse. The sixfold āmagandha—namely, unrestraint toward living beings, harming others, immorality, cruelty, harshness, and lack of regard—whether previously mentioned through the method of 'killing, slaughtering, cutting, binding,' or not yet mentioned, should be understood. The eating of meat is not āmagandha. Even though it was stated previously, it is spoken again for reasons such as the listeners' desire to hear, for their remembrance, and for the sake of strengthening their understanding. Therefore, it will be said later: 'The Blessed One explained this meaning again and again; He, the master of the Vedas, made it known.'

Among those beings, those who are 'giddhā' are those attached through greed; 'viruddhā' are those who oppose through hatred; 'atipātino' are those who take life by repeatedly falling into transgression without seeing the danger through delusion. Or, in the evil deeds mentioned through the method of 'killing, slaughtering, cutting, binding,' they are 'giddhā, viruddhā, and atipātino' through greed, opposition, and killing, which are known as lust, hatred, and delusion as they arise. 'Niccuyyutā' means those who are constantly exerted in committing unwholesome deeds and never refrain after reflection. 'Pecca' means after going from this world to the next. 'Those who go to darkness' (tamaṃ vajanti ye) refers to those who go to the darkness known as the interval between worlds (lokantarika) or to the darkness of being born into low families and so forth. 'Beings who fall head-first into hell' (patanti sattā nirayaṃ avaṃsirā) refers to those beings who fall into hells such as Avīci with their heads downward. The three types of āmagandha consisting of greed, opposition, and killing, which are the cause of those beings going to darkness and falling into hell, and which are the root of all āmagandha, are the only true āmagandha. The eating of meat, however, is not āmagandha.

Thus, the Blessed One, having explained āmagandha in the ultimate sense and having revealed it as the path to the states of misery (duggati), now, in order to show that the ascetic—who perceives the eating of fish and meat as āmagandha and as the path to misery, and who, desiring purity by not eating it, abstains from it—is unable to purify himself or others of that kind, spoke the six verses beginning with 'Na macchamaṃsaṃ.' In those verses:
307:
All phrases should be connected with the final phrase: 'Abstaining from fish and meat does not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt; performing sacrifices and seasonal observances do not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt'—this is how they should be connected. In this verse, 'na macchamaṃsaṃ' means that the non-eating of fish and meat does not purify a mortal. Similarly, the ancient teachers explain that the state of being one who does not eat fish and meat does not purify. However, it would be even better to interpret it thus: 'It is not the state of not eating fish and meat, nor is it the state of not not eating fish and meat; rather, the state of not eating fish and meat does not purify a mortal'—this is the meaning. If this is the case, one might ask: 'Will the state of not eating fish and meat then be diminished?' It cannot be diminished, because it is included within the practice of 'amaratapa' (asceticism for immortality). In the passage 'There are many amaratapa practices in the world,' it should be understood that all remaining forms of self-mortification (attakilamatha) mentioned are included. 

'Naggiyaṃ' means nakedness (acelakattaṃ). 'Muṇḍiyaṃ' means the state of having a shaven head (muṇḍabhāvo). 'Jaṭājallaṃ' means matted hair and the smearing of dust and dirt. 'Kharājināni' means rough antelope skins. 'Aggihuttassūpasevanā' means tending the sacrificial fire. 'Amarā' refers to the defilements of the body that arise from the longing for the state of immortality. 'Bahū' refers to many practices such as the practice of squatting and so forth. 'Tapā' refers to practices that torment the body. 'Mantā' refers to the Vedic scriptures. 'Āhutī' refers to the act of making fire offerings. 'Yaññamutūpasevanā' refers to sacrifices such as the Assamedha and the observance of the seasons. 'Observance of the seasons' means seeking out heat in the summer, staying at the foot of a tree in the rainy season, and entering the water in the winter. 

'Do not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt' means they cannot purify a mortal who is not yet free from doubt (vicikicchā), whether in terms of the purification of defilements or the purification of existence. Indeed, as long as the stain of doubt exists, one cannot be pure, and you yourself are still possessed of doubt. In this context, regarding the phrase 'one who has not crossed over doubt,' we do not hold the view that the Buddha spoke this because doubt arose in the ascetic as to whether 'the path of purification might be achieved through the non-eating of fish and meat, etc.' Rather, it should be understood that this was spoken in reference to the doubt that arose in the ascetic regarding the Buddha as soon as he heard that 'He [the Buddha] eats fish and meat.'

Having thus shown the inability of practices such as not eating fish and meat to bring about purification, the Buddha now spoke the verse beginning with 'Sotesu gutto' (Guarded in the senses) to show the qualities that are capable of bringing about purification. In that verse, 'sotesu' refers to the six sense faculties. 'Gutto' means being endowed with the protection of sense-restraint (indriyasaṃvara). By this much, He shows the virtue (sīla) that is the retinue of sense-restraint. 'Viditindriyo care' means that one should fare or dwell having known the six sense faculties through 'full understanding of the known' (ñātapariññā) and making them clear. By this much, He shows the discernment of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) of one who possesses pure virtue. 'Dhamme ṭhito' means being established in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths which are to be realized through the Noble Path. By this, He shows the stage of Stream-entry (sotāpatti).
308:
'Ajjavamaddave rato' means delighting in uprightness and gentleness. By this, He shows the stage of the Once-returner (sakadāgāmi). Indeed, a Once-returner delights in uprightness and gentleness because of the thinning out of greed and hatred, which cause crookedness of body and so forth, and which make the mind stubborn. 'Saṅgātigo' means one who has transcended the attachments of greed and hatred. By this, He shows the stage of the Non-returner (anāgāmi). 'Sabbadukkhappahīno' means one who has abandoned all suffering by abandoning the causes of the entire round of suffering (vaṭṭadukkha). By this, He shows the stage of Arahantship (arahatta). 'Na lippati diṭṭhasutesu dhīro' means that the wise one, having thus reached Arahantship in due order and being endowed with steadfastness, is no longer smeared by any defilement in things seen or heard. Not only is he not smeared by things seen and heard, but he is also not smeared by things sensed or cognized. On the contrary, he is one who has reached supreme purity—thus the Buddha concluded the teaching with Arahantship as its peak.

## 254-5. From here on, the two verses beginning with 'Iccetamattaṃ' were spoken by the Elders who conducted the Recital (Saṅgītikāras). The meaning of those verses is: Thus, the Blessed Kassapa Buddha explained, declared, and elaborated that matter again and again through many verses, using both teachings based on principles (dhammādhiṭṭhāna) and teachings based on persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), until that ascetic understood. 'Naṃ vedayi mantapāragū' means that Tissa the Brahmin ascetic, who had reached the end of the mantras and the end of the Vedas, also understood that meaning. For what reason? Because the Sage (Muni) revealed it through verses that were beautiful in meaning, in phrasing, and in the method of teaching. 

What kind of Dhamma was it? It is called 'nirāmagandha' (free from raw stench) because of the absence of the defilements known as 'āmagandha'. It is called 'asita' (unattached) because of the absence of dependence on craving and views. It is called 'durannaya' (difficult to track) because no one is able to lead him away by the power of external views, saying 'This is better, this is superior.' Having heard the well-spoken words of the Buddha who thus revealed it—having heard the Dhamma teaching that is free from raw stench, unyoked from defilements, and the dispeller of all suffering, the dispeller of all the suffering of the round—Tissa the Brahmin, with a humble mind, paid homage to the Tathāgata; he paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata by performing the five-point prostration. 'Tattheva pabbajjamarocayittha' means that right there, the ascetic Tissa requested the going-forth (pabbajjā) from the Blessed Kassapa who was seated on his seat; he begged for it. The Blessed One said to him, 'Ehi bhikkhu' (Come, monk). At that very moment, he became endowed with the eight requisites and, descending from the sky like an elder of a hundred years, he paid homage to the Blessed One. Within a few days, having penetrated the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), he became the Chief Disciple named Tissa. Later, the second [Chief Disciple] was named Bhāradvāja. Thus, that Blessed One had the pair of disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja.
309: Our Buddha brought together all fourteen verses—the three verses spoken first by the Brahmin Tissa, the nine verses spoken in the middle by the Blessed One Kassapa, and the two verses spoken at the end by the Reciters (Saṅgītikārakas) at that time—and, making them complete, he explained the Āmagandha Sutta, the teaching on 'inner stench,' to the five hundred ascetics led by their teacher. Having heard that discourse, the Brahmin became humble in mind, paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and requested ordination along with his followers. The Blessed One said, 'Come, monks (Ehi bhikkhavo).' They immediately attained the status of 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks, came through the air, paid homage to the Blessed One, and within a few days, all of them were established in the highest fruit, Arahantship. ## The Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā ## The Explanation of the Āmagandha Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is finished. ## 3. Explanation of the Hiri Sutta 'Hiriṃ tarantaṃ' and so forth is the Hiri Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising? Before the Buddha had appeared, there was a certain wealthy Great Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla) in Sāvatthī with a fortune of eighty crores. He had a beloved and dear only son. Although he raised the boy like a divine prince with various comforts and services, the Brahmin passed away along with his wife before he could hand over the wealth to his son. Then, after the death of the youth's parents, the treasurer opened the storehouse and, wishing to hand over the inheritance, said: 'Master, this is the property from your parents' time; this is the property of your grandfathers and great-grandfathers; this has come down through seven generations of the family.' When the youth saw the wealth, he thought: 'Only this wealth is seen; those who accumulated it are no longer seen; all have come under the power of death. And when they went, they could not take anything from here. Indeed, one must go to the next world having abandoned these enjoyments; it is not possible to take anything except for good conduct (sucarita). What if I were to give up this wealth and take the wealth of good conduct, which can be taken along?' Every day he spent a hundred thousand, and again he thought: 'This wealth is vast; how can it be fulfilled with such a small renunciation? ...'
310: 'What if I were to give a great almsgiving?' he thought. He informed the King: 'Great King, there is this much wealth in my house; I wish to give a great almsgiving with it. It would be good, Great King, if you would have a proclamation made in the city.' The King had it done as requested. Filling the vessels of all who came, he gave away all his wealth for seven days. After giving, he thought: 'After making such a great renunciation, it is not proper to live in a house; what if I were to go forth?' Then he informed his servants of this matter. They said, 'Master, do not think "My wealth is exhausted"; we will accumulate wealth again in a short time through various means,' and they pleaded with him in many ways. Without heeding their plea, he went forth as an ascetic (tāpasa). In that ascetic life, there are eight kinds of ascetics: (1) Saputtabhariya, (2) Uñchācārika, (3) Sampattakālika, (4) Anaggipakkika, (5) Asmamuṭṭhika, (6) Dantaluyyaka, (7) Pavattafalika, and (8) Vaṇṭamuttika. Among these eight, the Saputtabhariya are those like the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya, who go forth with their wives and children and make a living through farming, trade, and so forth. The Uñchācārika are those who have a hermitage built at the city gate, teach arts and sciences to princes and Brahmin youths there, reject gold and silver, and accept only allowable items (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) such as sesame and rice. These are superior to the Saputtabhariya ascetics. The Sampattakālika are those who sustain themselves by taking whatever food is obtained at the time of eating. These are superior to the Uñchācārika ascetics. The Anaggipakkika are those who sustain themselves by eating leaves and fruits that are not cooked by fire. These are superior to the Sampattakālika ascetics. The Asmamuṭṭhika are those who wander carrying a stone hammer or other small knives, and when hungry, take bark from a tree they reach, eat it, undertake the factors of the Uposatha, and develop the four Brahma-vihāras. These are superior to the Anaggipakkika ascetics. The Dantaluyyaka are those who wander without even carrying stone hammers and so forth, and when hungry, peel off bark with their teeth from a tree they reach, eat it, undertake the factors of the Uposatha, and develop the Brahma-vihāras. These are superior to the Asmamuṭṭhika ascetics. The Pavattafalika are those who live depending on a lake or a forest grove, eating whatever lotus stalks or roots are in the lake, or flowers when it is flowering season, or fruits when it is fruiting season in the forest grove. When there are no flowers or fruits, they live by eating at least the tree bark there; they do not go elsewhere for the sake of food.
311:
They observe the factors of the Uposatha and practice the development of the Brahma-vihāras; these (Pavattaphalika) ascetics are superior to the Dantaluyyaka ascetics. Those called Vaṇṭamuttika eat only leaves that have fallen from their stalks to the ground; the rest of their practice is the same as before; these ascetics are the most excellent of all.

This young man of a Brahmin family thought, "I will undertake the highest form of renunciation among the ascetic renunciations," and having become a Vaṇṭamuttika ascetic, he crossed two or three mountains in the Himavanta and built a hermitage where he resided. At that time, the Blessed One had appeared in the world, set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, and in due course arrived at Sāvatthī, staying at the Jetavana monastery, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī. At that time, a man living in Sāvatthī, while searching for sandalwood heartwood and such on the mountains, reached the ascetic's hermitage, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. Seeing him, the ascetic asked, "Where have you come from?" "From Sāvatthī, venerable sir," he replied. "What news is there from there?" he asked. "Venerable sir, the people there are diligent and perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)," he replied. "Whose instruction do they follow in doing so?" he asked. "They follow the instruction of the Blessed Buddha," he replied. Hearing the word "Buddha," the ascetic was amazed and asked three times, in the manner described in the Āmagandha Sutta, "O man, did you say 'Buddha'?" Thinking, "Even this sound is rare in the world," he became joyful and, wishing to go to the Blessed One, thought, "It is not proper to go to the Buddha empty-handed; what should I take with me?" Then he thought, "Buddhas do not care for material gifts; I will take a gift of the Dhamma," and he prepared four questions:

What kind of friend should not be associated with? What kind of friend should be associated with?
What kind of effort (payoga) should be exerted? Among tastes, which taste is the most excellent?

Taking those questions, he set out towards the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) and in due course reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jetavana monastery. At that time, the Blessed One was seated on his designated seat to teach the Dhamma. Seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic stood at a respectful distance without paying homage. The Blessed One greeted him, saying, "Ascetic, is it bearable for you?" and so on. The ascetic also replied, "Venerable Gotama, it is bearable," and so on, and then thought, "If he is truly the Buddha, he will answer with speech the questions I ask in my mind." He then asked those questions to the Blessed One only in his mind. When the Blessed One was thus questioned by the Brahmin (ascetic)...
312: To answer the first question first, starting with the words 'Hiriṃ tarantaṃ,' he spoke two and a half verses (gāthās). The meaning of those verses is: 'Hiriṃ tarantaṃ' means one who transgresses the sense of shame, who is shameless, who lacks shame regarding evil deeds. 'Vijigucchamānaṃ' means one who views [shame] with disgust, like excrement. A shameless person is disgusted by shame and views it like excrement; therefore, he does not associate with or cling to it. Thus it is said, 'vijigucchamānaṃ.' 'Tavāhamasmi' means one who speaks only with words, saying, 'Friend, I am your companion, I wish for your welfare and happiness, I have even sacrificed my life for your sake,' and so on. 'Sayhāni kammāni anādiyantaṃ' means one who, despite saying such things, does not undertake or commit to performing the tasks of a friend that he is capable of. Or, it refers to one who does not pay serious attention in his heart and, when tasks arise, shows only ruin. A wise man should know, 'This person is not my good friend, but only a false friend.' 'Ananvayaṃ' means that although he says, 'I will give, I will do,' it does not happen according to what he says. He is one who speaks pleasant words to friends only with a mere appearance of affection, using useless words about the past and future. Wise men distinguish and know, 'This person is a false friend called vacīparama (one who excels only in speech),' who does not do what he says, but speaks only with words. 'One who is always looking for ruin, staying close with sweet words, and without being negligent, watches for faults, thinking, "When will he blame me? Then I will accuse him back with this point," is not a friend to be associated with.' Thus, the Blessed One answered the first question, 'What kind of friend should not be associated with?' and to answer the second question, he spoke the half-verse starting with 'Yasmiñca seti'.
313:
The meaning of that verse is: In whichever friend a friend enters the heart and sleeps, just as a son sleeps on his father's breast, without hesitation or suspicion, thinking, "While I sleep on this breast, will there be suffering or displeasure for this father?" and so forth; even so, placing trust in wife, wealth, life, and so on, he sleeps (lives) without suspicion in the state of friendship. Whichever friend cannot be divided (broken) by others even if they speak a hundred or a thousand reasons, that person should indeed be known as a friend to be associated with.

Thus the Blessed One, having answered the second question, "What kind of friend should be associated with?", spoke the verse beginning with "Pāmuzzakaraṇaṃ" to answer the third question. The meaning of that verse is: It is called "pāmuzzakaraṇa" because it causes joy (pāmuzza). "Ṭhāna" means cause. What is that cause? It is energy (vīriya). Indeed, that energy is called "pāmuzzakaraṇa" because it produces joy, gladness, and happiness associated with the Dhamma. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, whichever monk has aroused energy, he dwells happily." It is called "pasaṃsāvahana" because it brings praise. It is called "sukha" (happiness) by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), because it brings the happiness of devas and humans in the beginning, and the happiness of Nibbāna in the end. It is called "phalānisaṃsa" because it longs for the fruit. "Bhāveti" means to develop (increase). "Vahanto porisaṃ dhuraṃ" means while dwelling by carrying the burden suitable for men, he develops this state called right exertion (sammappadhāna-vīriya); such an application (payoga) should be practiced.

Thus the Blessed One, having answered the third question, "What kind of effort should be practiced?", spoke the verse beginning with "Pavivekarasaṃ" to answer the fourth question. In that verse, "paviveka" (seclusion) refers to the noble fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) because it arises from seclusion from defilements. Its "rasa" (taste) is the happiness (sukha) associated with that fruit in the sense of being enjoyed. "Upasama" (peace) is also that same fruit of Arahatship, either because it arises when defilements are stilled or because it has the peace called Nibbāna as its object. "Dhammapītirasa" (the taste of joy in the Dhamma) is also that same fruit of Arahatship, because it is not separate from the noble Dhamma and because it is the taste of joy arisen in the Dhamma called Nibbāna. Having drunk that taste of seclusion and the taste of peace, and drinking that very taste of joy in the Dhamma, one becomes free from distress and sinless. Even after drinking, one is free from distress because of the absence of the fever of defilements; even while drinking, one is sinless because of having abandoned evil (pāpa). Therefore, this taste is the supreme among tastes. However, some teachers say: "By virtue of jhāna, Nibbāna, and reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), or by virtue of seclusion of body (kāya-viveka), seclusion of mind (citta-viveka), and seclusion from substrata (upadhi-viveka), these three states such as the taste of seclusion are only three."
